subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS FOR APPOINTMENTS TO BE MADE THIS WEEK
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Labour when it is anticipated that appointments will be made to positions on the national war labour board?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS FOR APPOINTMENTS TO BE MADE THIS WEEK
speechtext: It is anticipated that these appointments will be made almost immediately. May I explain that any delay in the appointments is not due to any action of the government. REGULATIONS WrITH RESPECT TO EXPORT OF HERRING
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries in relation to the order in council, passed in August last, under which the fisheries regulations were amended in so far as they relate to the province of New Brunswick, and which provided for the banning of the export of herring between January 1 and April 15 in each year. As he is aware, the matter has been under reconsideration- if that is a proper term to use-and I was informed that a meeting was held in the United States recently-this very last week. I want to know if it has now been decided to rescind the regulation, or what the position is.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext: The matter is still under advisement. Negotiations are being carried on with the United States authorities with a view of satisfying all concerned.
"Satisfying all concerned"! That means that you are going to rescind it; that is the only way to satisfy them.

subtopic: BALLOT IN FORD MOTOR COMPANY PLANT-LETTER OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMPANY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BALLOT IN FORD MOTOR COMPANY PLANT-LETTER OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMPANY
speechtext:
I wish to ask the Minister of Labour if his attention has been drawn to an advertisement which appeared in, I believe, the Windsor Star on the seventh of this month. A copy of the page has been sent, I understand, to hon. members. I am not going to read the advertisement, but I wish to draw attention to a copy of a letter which has been inserted in the advertisement, and which has been sent by the president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada to each employee of the company at Windsor. The letter has to do with the organization of the employees in the plant. It begins:
Let's discuss this organization question, man to man.
You have been approached, or will be approached, by organizers urging you to sign up with a certain union.
Everyone knows what they promise.
Then it says that this will cost the employees $150,000 a year. Further on in the letter, as it appears in the advertisement, it is stated:
The impartial services of the Department of Labour of the dominion government are avail-
Labour Conditions

able for just such a purpose. Under their supervision a committee of employees can be nominated and elected by secret ballot. This ballot would give every man a chance to express his real opinion on this question.
Has this been drawn to the minister's attention, and if it has, does he not think that it violates or contravenes paragraph 6 of order in council P.C. 2685, which states:
That employees should be free to organize in trade unions, free from any control by employers or their agents.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: BALLOT IN FORD MOTOR COMPANY PLANT-LETTER OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not see the
advertisement. I do not know that it is necessary for me to go into it in any great detail at the present time. The reason is this. Both employers and employees agreed that they would hold a ballot under the auspices of the Department of Labour. Those auspices have been provided. The form of the ballot has been agreed upon. I believe that every detail in connection with the vote has been agreed upon between the employers and the employees; if there is any detail outstanding it is a very small one. The vote is to take place on Thursday. I do not think that I can go further than to say that those representing the union to which the hon. member for Vancouver East has referred have expressed their complete approval of all the arrangements that have been made; and so has the company.

subtopic: BALLOT IN FORD MOTOR COMPANY PLANT-LETTER OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMPANY
speechtext: The minister did not answer my question. I asked him whether this did not violate or contravene P.C. 2685- interference with the employees in forming a union of their own choice.

subtopic: BALLOT IN FORD MOTOR COMPANY PLANT-LETTER OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMPANY
speechtext: The suggestion was made by the company that a vote be taken to obtain the wish of the employees of the company as to whether or not they desired to join a particular union. The union said, "That is perfectly fair; we are willing to have a vote taken to determine whether or not the majority of the employees of this plant wish to join this union." Surely there is no violation of order in council P.C. 2685, or any other, in a mutual agreement on the part of the company and the employees, who decide that this is the fairest method of determining the wishes of the employees themselves.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE-TRANSFER OF FUNDS TO THE UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE-TRANSFER OF FUNDS TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) asked a question with regard to remittances of funds by representatives of labour unions in Canada to head offices or other offices of labour unions in the United States. The question was connected with one relating to the International Labour Office, and that part of the question may have been completely answered by the Prime Minister. However, I have here a complete reply which I will now give.
As the Prime Minister stated yesterday, the International Labour Organization is an intergovernmental body and the arrangements regarding the operations of its bank accounts as set out in the Canada Gazette of October 25 confirm the international status of these accounts and in general place them on the same basis as the accounts of diplomatic representatives of foreign countries. As the members of the house are no doubt aware, the International Labour Organization is a part of the League of Nations which formerly had its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland. When it became impossible to carry out the important duties of this body from Geneva the director of the International Labour Organization accepted in the summer of 1940 an invitation from McGill university to establish a working centre in Montreal.
As a matter of interest to the house, I would mention that the budget of the International Labour Organization is established in a hard currency, namely, Swiss francs. Their expenses in Canada over and above the portion covered by the regular annual contribution of the Canadian government are met from the proceeds of the sale of hard currency to the foreign exchange control board. This is in effect a transfer of United States

The War-Mr. Harris (Danforth)
funds to Canada. The establishment of a working centre of the International Labour Organization in Montreal therefore has the incidental effect of bringing United States exchange into the country.
The hon. member for Parkdale will realize that the arrangements made for the International Labour Organization do not grant any privileges or concessions to the Committee for Industrial Organization or other similar labour bodies.
The government's policy is to provide foreign exchange for the payment of fees, dues or other normal contributions in connection with membership in all recognized international professional, occupational or fraternal organizations. These include such organizations as international service clubs, fraternal societies, trade and professional associations as well as international labour unions. All these various types of international organizations are treated on exactly the same basis and no preferred treatment is given to any one of them.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. ILSLEY PRESS REPORT AS TO TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. ILSLEY PRESS REPORT AS TO TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. A press report 14873-268
published on November 4, purporting to set out the travelling expenses of various ministers of the government, gave the travelling expenses of the Minister of Finance for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, as $17,257-that is, for the Minister of Finance and secretaries. For the previous year ended March 31, 1940, the amount given was $544. So far as I am concerned-and I was Minister of National Revenue part of the time and Minister of Finance for another part-the figures are as follows: For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1940, for myself and two secretaries, $1,743.62; for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, $585 for myself and nothing for secretaries.
This information is contained in sessional paper No. 335. I mention this merely because the statement is receiving some circulation, particularly in my province, and it has been suggested that unless it is corrected it might possibly have some detrimental effect on the war savings campaign.

Canada's war effort
The house again in committee of the whole, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

As I came into the chamber I saw staring me in the face "November 11", and I thought back some twenty-three short years ago to another November 11. What a change, what a difference, Mr. Chairman, in two decades! Did we go far enough twenty-three years ago? I doubt it very much. Are we going far enough to-day? I say, nay; we are not going far enough. We are not doing all that we are capable of doing. In the last decade there have been voids, not of a day or of a month, but of a year when we were not at our task in furtherance of the things we hold dear. I do not purpose to sound a note of criticism or say anything to belittle the effort that is now being made. I do not purpose to recite history or geography; we have had enough of that. But we have not had nearly enough about what we are going to do in the present emergency. We all know that we failed during the last decade. We all know where the responsibility lies; I am not going to recite it. We all know from our press and other sources of information what has taken place. When I think of the state of Europe I am impelled to say a word on the state of our nation, the state of democracy, the state of our empire. But first let me deal for a moment with Europe.



The War-Mr. Harris (Danjorth)
The first minister of the crown gave you the history and the geography up to the present, and then he stopped. It has been my privilege to know something of Europe. A dozen of the capital cities of former independent states are to-day under the heel of Hitler. From the Arctic to the Aegean, from the walls of Moscow to the Pyrenees, the people of Europe are under the heel of Hitler. Who are the people who are under that heel? We know them-broad-backed, short-legged men and women who have known nothing for many generations but hard work; two hundred million of them enslaved to a hundred million slave-drivers. Yet on all sides we see signs in our land of a lack of continued effort. We find the power of this chamber not harnessed to-day, this chamber which is the detonator or sounding-board of the nation, this chamber which is the only free expression of opinion in Canada. Sitting here to-day many hon. members feel that they ought to be out of here, ought to be at home, that they are not doing any good here. They feel that perhaps this is not the way to inspire the nation. That sounding-board in the fourth estate cannot refuse to disseminate what is placed on the record of Hansard. It will not be censored; it will be recorded freely in a censored press. It may be repeated over the radio and it may be of some consequence in helping us to call for an all-out effort. I do not criticize too much the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); I know he has to be away from this chamber a good deal. As I said some years ago, the ministers of the crown should have some kind of organization that would relieve them of the necessity of sitting here long hours; they should have deputies or undersecretaries to carry out the little duties so that the ministers themselves could come in to attend to the big duties.
Sitting opposite me to-day is the Minister of Munitions and Supply, operating the biggest industrial enterprise that Canada ever knew; indeed I am of the opinion that the industry of which he is managing director is the greatest on the north American continent. Why should he have to sit here and listen to speeches such as he had to listen to yesterday? I take full responsibility for what I found it necessary to say, and more and more is going to be said. But the responsibility for such a set-up as we have is on our present organization. I say to the Prime Minister: there are men within your own ranks, and hon. members on this side, who are well able and anxious to do something on behalf of Canada. Inspire them; use them; put them to work. The Prime Minister, speaking of a
	T|
certain committee, said that it afforded an opportunity for hon. members of the House of Commons to do some useful work. In the operations of the war expenditures committee, what opportunity was given? None. Was it fair; was it set up in such a way that it could be of real service? It did some good. What took place during those hot days of June, July, August and September? What was being done in the supposed centre of all activity in Canada-Ottawa? I said on one occasion, and I reiterate it now, that Ottawa was like a morgue. Who was chairman of that committee? A member of the government. First they thought of subdividing the committee into five; then when it was apparent that four members of the official opposition could not be divided into five parts they made it three, so that we had one member on each subcommittee, except one on which we had two. So that a member of the official opposition could- move a motion, but was often unable to find a seconder. The committee was improperly formed; the electorate of Canada was not equally represented, and we did not have the opportunity of doing all the work we would like to have done. But I shall have more to say on that a little later.
On this occasion I want my remarks to be more appropriate to the day-this sacred day, Remembrance day. I point out to the Prime Minister and the government that our people are looking for more leadership, not only from the Prime Minister but from all of us. It seems to me that we in Canada and in this house are acting like people in the bleachers at a football match. We are watching the game. Wre are watching Russia, watching Germany; our spirits go up and down; we do not seem to realize that we ourselves are in the game. We are coming to the semifinals. One by one those opposed to totalitarianism have been defeated. To-day with our wishful thinking we are hoping that Russia will hold out. Very shortly the finals are coming. Where are we going to be then? Will our people be so firmly joined in a united effort that we can give a good account of ourselves? Those of us who are gathered together in this chamber have a direct responsibility to see to it that our people are doing everything possible. But you cannot discharge that responsibility if you go to your homes and let this House of Commons sink back into the moribund state which existed here between the close of June and the beginning of November. We have no right to go home until we point the way in all our activities, and until our people feel that we are doing everything we possibly can do.

The War-Mr. Harris (Danjorth)
When I think of the strength of those opposing democracy it frightens me, and I am not one who is easily frightened. When I think- and I say this in all kindness-of the weakness of our national effort, led by the present administration, it frightens me. Why do I say that? Not because the Minister of Justice is ill and absent from his place.; not because the Minister of Transport is ill. I have a profound respect for those hon. gentlemen; I am sorry they are not here, but because they are ill Hitler has not stopped the war. Someone should be found not to replace them but to take charge of their departments; and I would not limit it to that. I am thinking of what these two hon. gentlemen mean, and what they represent, to one quarter of our population, people who were citizens of Canada long before many of us were Canadians, whose families have been in this country for many generations. What they feel in their minds and hearts is not being fully represented in this chamber. In all possible kindness I say to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot): You may reflect some of the sentiment in your province, but you are only human and you cannot reflect it all. We need all the inspiration it is possible to get during these very difficult and trying times.
Let us to-day, then, rededicate ourselves one and all to the cause which concerns us day and night. Let no word of mine be regarded as of a pessimistic nature. I want to be realistic all through this difficult time. I want to know what is happening. Several hon. gentlemen opposite have been in England. All those who have been there should tell those of us who have not had that privilege exactly what is in their hearts. To-day I speak from my heart, from my head, and from the very depths of my soul, just rambling on trying to tell you how I feel about the state of our nation. If we must have a closed session in order that those who have been there may tell us what is going on, let it be a closed session. I take second place to no one in this chamber in my desire that everything for the good of the nation should be discussed in open session. I have had some experience during the last few months in that regard, and I have not altered my point of view; but if the Prime Minister in his judgment says we should have a closed session if we are to have the truth, then let us have a secret session. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, are the men in this chamber my colleagues or must I listen to their stories told in whispers, and draw my own conclusions? During the twenty years I have sat here I have thought, and still think, that the mem-14873-268}
bers of this house are my colleagues. What I know that is in the interests of the nation, they should know; what they know that is in the interests of the nation, I should know. Otherwise I am not able to serve to the best of my ability. I do not want to listen to scandalmongers on street comers as to what is happening over there. I want to listen to those who have been there; and I demand of the administration now that my request be given consideration.
We get information from other sources, of course, and we reveal that information in this chamber so that the nation in turn may know what is going on. I received a letter only last evening from Welwyn Garden City, Herts, England. This letter is from the managing director's office of a very large concern in London; it is dated 21/10/41, and is postmarked Ottawa, November 10. It reached Ottawa last night. This is what the writer says:
And so this wretched war drags on! The feeling here is just this. We would far sooner die than yield to a tyranny that we think would be far worse than death. But we just don't intend to die quietly at the hands of the hun. We shall fight him if he conies, and we shall beat him. He will never, no never, take this island home of ours. I am, my dear Joe, assured, as you say, that you are all with us in this fight, to a man, and this is a great inspiration to us. God bless you and yours.
A quarter of a century ago the battle was raging at Vimy. Where will it be raging soon; on the Sussex downs? If we fail, all fail; if we fall, all fall, according to some of our great statesmen. Therefore, speaking as an ordinary member of the Canadian House of Commons, and guaranteeing all the cooperation I can give at this time, I say: recognize us; acknowledge us; inspire us; shame us; enthuse us; exalt us; employ us; drive us; order us; command us; criticize us; approve us; disapprove us; chastize us; listen to us; possess us; dispossess us; control us; charge us; bankrupt us; pauperize us; cheer us; free us; prepare us; dedicate us; rededicate us; bereave us; conscript us, and for God's sake lead us.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Chairman, yesterday I drew the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the fact that it was rather difficult to deal with the various departments as single units. We are now dealing with the Department of Munitions and Supply.
Knowing something of the manufacturing industry in Canada, may I say that I do not
The War-Mr. Homuth

know of any minister who has a more difficult job, or who is getting more cooperation from the manufacturers and workmen in Canada, than the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). He has a tremendous task, a task which is not particularly associated with government policy. His job is to get munitions and more munitions. The only part of it connected with the general administration of the government is the effect that the Department of Labour, Department of Finance or the Department of National Defence may have on the production of the munitions he requires.
So that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is not particularly concerned with government policy, except as it may affect him. I repeat, he has a tremendous task. He has many able men surrounding him. Sometimes I wonder how they handle the task which has been given them. On many occasions I have had to appear before officers in that department in connection with difficulties arising in industries in my own constituency. Waterloo county is a highly industrialized section of Canada. I have found those officials anxious to do everything they could to help the minister, and to help in our war effort.
But in dealing with his department we must also deal with the departments of labour and finance. Let me give an example of how those departments are dovetailed. When war broke out most industries realized that there would be an increase in the cost of living. Heads of industries who were fair to their employees-and most of them are-immediately put into effect either a bonus system or an increased basic rate of wages. Later on an order in council was passed by the Department of Labour making it mandatory that industries dealing directly with the government give a cost of living bonus. The plea went out to industries which were not dealing directly with the government that they also give a cost of living bonus, so as to avoid strife between industry and labour in Canada. Most of the industries responded to that request.
What happened? During the last session, when the increase in the national defence tax became effective, pleas were made by hon. members on this side of the house that in levying the national defence tax, and in the compilation of income tax, exemption up to a certain amount should be allowed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) accepted the idea that married men without children should be exempted up to SI,200. Then the Department of Labour issued the plea that a cost of living bonus should be paid. Hundreds of employees in my district were granted the cost of living bonus, at that time computed at

the rate of five per cent. On the basis of that percentage a bonus of $60 a year was to be paid to married men earning SI ,200. That was done because the Department of Labour pointed out that it would cost those people S60 a year more to live. Then the Minister of Finance came along and said, "Now that you are getting $1,260 a year I shall have to levy on you a tax of five per cent." And so the Department of Finance took from the man who, on the plea of the Minister of Labour, had been given a cost of living bonus, the bonus which had been given to him. Actually the tax would have amounted to $63, but the Department of Finance could take from an employee only an amount sufficient to bring him back to his $1,200 basis. The same principle applies to single people.
It appears therefore that we have two departments acting differently. One department pleads with the industries in this country to treat its employees fairly, and when they are about to do so the Department of Finance comes along and takes from them what the Department of Labour has asked industry to give them.
I had thought that when the house reassembled, in view of the fact that so much had been done by order in council-and I realize the necessity for it-we would have prorogued and begun a new session. These measures had been tried out for a year or more, and, from the experience we have had in their operation, they could have been amended so as to give the people some assurance that members of the House of Commons are trying to treat *them fairly.
Employees have come to my office-and they come to the offices of all industries in my district-and have said, "We do not want your cost of living bonus, because the government is taking it away from us anyway." If the government is taking $60 from a man, does not that deduction constitute an increase in the cost of living? Is that not one more of the factors which cause inflation? We are attempting to put a ceiling on prices and on wages, and to stop inflation. Yet this very lack of cooperation among departments is doing much to bring about inflation. When the Prime Minister stated that we would sit for a week or two to give members of the cabinet an opportunity to present prepared statements, which would be laid open for discussion- despite the fact that, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, although we can discuss them we can get nowhere because we cannot move resolutions or amendments-he pointed out that, having regard to the convenience of members and the difficulties of obtaining accommodation in the city, we should then adjourn to meet

The War-Mr. Homuth
again in January. When any man offers himself as a candidate for the House of Commons he ought to know something of what his responsibility will be. He knows what his indemnity is going to be and if he does not know what call is to be made upon him when he tries for a seat in the House of Commons he should be prepared to make whatever sacrifice may be necessary. It does not matter whether we sit here three months or six months or twelve months; we are at war and we ought to be here attending to the business of the country.
As I say, we have had an opportunity of studying the working out of many of these laws. We have been able to see something of what lack of foresight on the part of the government is doing to industry and to recruiting in this country. A national registration was taken. True, that was long months after it had been urged in the house, but eventually it was done. If the cards are checked carefully it will be found that hundreds of outstanding machinists are to-day driving bakery and milk wagons or doing other types of less strenuous jobs. If we had taken full advantage of the national registration act and had gone carefully over the answers given to the questions asked, we would have found that hundreds of thousands of young men could be placed in industry where they are vitally needed. But the only advantage we took of that registration was to call men up for war service.
Let us see what happened to the recruiting campaign in this country. When war was declared a fever of loyalty swept across the country and tens of thousands of young Canadians came forward to offer their services. But the government could not take them; they had no means of training them, they had no equipment, and there were no places in which they could be trained. They were sent home and told to come back. They were told, "We will call you when we want you." The feeling of loyalty which had swept across the country was dampened and died down. We then went on and recruited as we saw fit and as we were able to handle the men.
Finally the national war services act was passed, giving the government of the day the power to call men for service in Canada. Then the thirty-day training period was started, one of the worst money wasters we have had in this war effort. Men who were called up for this thirty-day training period have not been called up since and likely will not be called up to take further training. This represented a waste of millions of dollars, but it was an experience. Then the government decided that we should have a four months training period. Before the first four months training period was concluded the government, realizing the dangers and difficulties ahead, decided that they would conscript the men for home defence for the duration of the war. Enlistment fell off. We listened to a great many speeches by members of the government who, on the one hand, said that plenty of men were coming forward, that there was no dearth of soldiers or air force or naval men, and, on the other hand, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and high ranking officers of the army pleaded for men to come and fill up the ranks. They told us of the necessity for more and more men in order to defeat Hitler. In the meantime the papers were publishing stories of how the whole personnel in various training camps had enlisted, and there was on the part of the people of Canada a sense of security and a feeling that everything was all right.
During the summer months the Prime Minister went on a speaking tour in western Canada. While that tour was in progress, from many parts of the country came a cry for conscription, and from other parts of the country came a cry for selective service. The cry became so vocal that of necessity the Prime Minister had to answer it. On platform after platform in western Canada he said, "I have given my pledge to the people of Canada that I am opposed to the conscription of the men of Canada for service overseas, and I intend to abide by that promise."
Hear, hear.

Do not yell "hear, hear," too soon. Speaking in Calgary the Prime Minister said:
Those, howrever, who could serve, and who do not answer the call, will bear through life the stamp of that failure. Their neighbours will know; and, what is far worse, they themselves will know', in their hearts, that they have failed to seize the greatest opportunity which is likely ever to come to men to serve their country and their fellow' men.
In other words, "Unless those of you who are physically fit and of military age are prepared to offer your services for overseas in this crisis, the finger of shame will be pointed at you." Regardless of what our families may have done, regardless of what many of our loved ones may have done, there are many sitting in this chamber who did not serve in the last war. I did not serve in the last war, and other members of this party did not. The Prime Minister did not serve, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) did not, and there are other members of this house wbn
The War-Mr. Homuth

did not. But we have since been elected to the House of Commons, to an important position in the life of the nation. We did not serve in the last war, but the finger of shame was not pointed at us because we did not. Surely that is not the way to stir up the loyalty and enthusiasm of the young men who we feel ought to be serving overseas in the fighting forces of this country.
Later on in the same address the Prime Minister said:
Let us keep these truths ever before our young men; explain the need and the greatness of service, and no compulsion will be required to fill the ranks of Canada's overseas army.
We have the Prime Minister living up to the promise which he made to the electors, and we have him saying to the young men of this country, "If you do not enlist, all the rest of your life you will be ashamed of the part that you played."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if he is reading the text of a speech of mine, or is he placing his own interpretation upon what I said?
I am reading a report from the Prime Minister's own newspaper, the Toronto Star.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I wish to say to my hon. friend that with respect to men enlisting for service overseas I made no reference of the kind to which he refers. I have said repeatedly that any young man in this country who does not recognize the seriousness of the existing situation and play his part in helping to meet it is going to suffer for it in one way or another during the rest of his days.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Danforth says that the member for Temiscouata speaks only for his own constituency. Well, each of us has a double duty in this house. The first duty of every member is to represent the constituents who have honoured him with their confidence and honoured him by listening to his speeches during election time, and also by taking the trouble to go to the polls to mark their ballots in his favour. But members also represent Canada at large, because each member of parliament must realize that every time he discusses legislation, every time he gives his vote, he must do so not only from the parochial point of view of looking after his constituents, but also from the broader standpoint of the welfare of all Canadians. That is the point of view that members should take, and I am sure that my hon. friend the member for Danforth, as well as other members on either side, have such a point of view when they address the house or speak in committee, or whenever they rise to give their vote on any measure that is submitted to us.
There should be a general understanding about conscription, provided that necessary distinctions are made. We hear people say that we must have conscription, and by conscription they mean only conscription for overseas service. They do not regard the taking of men for service in Canada as conscription; conscription, according to them, is only for service overseas. I remember in 1939 at the special session I made a certain remark and one of the war ministers smiled. I said that I never conceived-and I cannot conceive it now-how it was that whereas the area of Canada is so large and that of England is so small, and whereas the population of England is so dense and that of Canada so small, we cannot keep our men in Canada for the possible eventual defence of this country, but that, as a matter of patriotism, we must send them overseas. I cannot conceive it. I think it shows a complete lack of proportion and is an insult to the courage of the British people. In fact, an outstanding publisher in England, a man who ranks very high in politics, once made this statement to me: Do you not think, you Canadians, that we Englishmen can look after the defence of our own island? We are just as brave as you are, and although we do not wish to offend you by telling you to return home when you come in the Canadian army, we do not need you here. We have enough valiant men among ourselves to defend our shores, to defend our island, just as we see to the defence of British trade on the high seas. Your duty is not to come here to share with us the food that is convoyed at such high 
cost; your duty is to stay at home and save us the trouble of having to defend Canada, which is so large a country. And he added these words, which should be remembered by every member of this house. He said: Your duty is not in the British isles, your duty is in Canada; look after Canada and we can look after the British isles. That man was a great Englishman, and his words put to shame many of the fake patriots who think only of sending the cream of our youth to England, causing embarrassment rather than helping.
Now, there is something else. All those who are in favour of conscription are not angels. I do not mean by that bad angels or good; I mean they are not spiritual beings. They need food to sustain them. That food has to be carried to their homes, sometimes from far distant places. What is the duty of the farmer in that instance? The duty of the farmer in time of war as well as in time of peace is to assure by his work that every Canadian and everyone in this country shall receive the food necessary for his subsistence. And of course when a man holds a rifle in England or is assigned to certain duty in England he cannot fulfil that great work here in Canada. Not only that; I am all for the National Resources Mobilization Act; I am all for total war effort, provided that everyone is assigned to his own proper post to ensure a complete and a quick victory over our common foe. Therefore why disturb the economic and social structure of this country? I cannot understand it.
The Union government promised the farmers that they would be exempt from conscription, not because they were cowards, as I have said before, but because they had an important work to do, the work of feeding both the army and the civilian population, and also of exporting food to the British isles-and now to Russia. That is the duty of the farmer. The fisherman has a similar duty. Why not exploit our fisheries in time of war as well as in time of peace? What is the duty of the railway employee, the man who has charge of a train, whether freight or passenger? His duty is to be here.
This, sir, is what I have said repeatedly; that the war should be carried on not on the basis of sentimentalism but on the basis of reason. The successes that the Germans have achieved in some parts of Europe are not due to sentimentalism, although they started their propaganda that way; they are based on strict reasoning. I appreciate the stand taken by my chief and by his government, to look after the defence of Canada; nothing too much can be done in that regard.

The War-Mr. Pouliot
I have a word to say to my Englishspeaking friends. I as a Frenck-Canadian have never uttered a word about religious or racial differences in the house. I respect the religious views of my colleagues, I respect their opinions, I respect them as men, and I want to enjoy the same respect myself. But there is one thing I will tell them; that is the only way to ensure national unity. We shall have national unity in this country only when our English-speaking fellow citizens will have the same sentiment and the same feeling for Great Britain as we have for France. There may be cultural relations with other lands, but we must think first of Canada, our common country, and our north American civilization, which does so much for the development of the mind as well as for the comfort of the body. Our American civilization now is much higher than the civilization of Europe, although Europe has led us in the past.
The very best and most stable element we have in this country is not found in the cities. It is the rural population, and so long as the rural people do their work in the future as they have in the past by helping this country to carry on the war, doing work which is just as useful as the work done in the munitions factories, then they should be considered as a class that must be kept at work without being disturbed or perturbed. I do not say that because I am a fifth columnist. Hon. members know what offers I made to the government, although they were not accepted at the time, but I am not grouching because I was refused. I want this country to win the war, and I want the people of this country to be healthy enough to do the very best job that can be done. That is why I do not want only unfits to be in charge of very important and very strenuous and difficult work.	Should we send
overseas only those who are healthy while men who are in bad physical condition, who are sick, who suffer from tuberculosis, hernia or goitre, will take their jobs? What happens? I speak very seriously through you, Mr. Chairman, to hon. gentlemen opposite as well as to those on this side of the house. It means that the health standard of this country will go lower and lower, and our war effort will decrease in the same proportion.
I took the trouble, at the request of the federation of mayors, to go to various cities of the United States to study the admirable work that has been done by the WPA under that great man, President Roosevelt, for the betterment of the health of the working classes. I reported to the mayors of the 14873-269
principal cities of my country and summarized that report in the house. But some hon. members, even including the leader of the opposition, said they did not see why I was giving so many figures. I praise very highly the Minister of Pensions and National Health for the new policies of his department, the purpose of which is to improve the health of our people. Of course they still suffer privations, and what may surprise you, sir, is that in the rural districts the people abide much more strictly by the regulations to save bacon and other foods to help our allies in this war than the people do in the cities. I commend the minister for giving a new direction to his department to improve the health of our fellow citizens.
There is something else also. In past years I obtained from the Department of National Defence sortie used clothing which was distributed to settlers and unemployed people in the outlying districts of my constituency. Some of these clothes were cut down for younger children, in order that they might be warmly clothed during our Canadian winter. This year, unfortunately, because of certain misunderstandings and because some hon. members who were sitting on a committee did not know what was done with this clothing, I have been unable to obtain any of these articles. It was my idea to start with the youth, to provide young Canadians with warm clothing in order that they might enjoy our healthy Canadian winter, and I hope those concerned will understand better in the future. I must also express my thanks to the deputy minister of the Department of National Defence for the assistance he has given me in the past in this regard. This clothing was not used for political propaganda; it was given to Tories as well as Liberals, to all those who needed help. We are all Canadians in this country.
It is no use talking about leadership. I could mention a good many jokes about the new leader of the Conservative party, and perhaps a few about the present leader, but I shall refrain from doing so on a day such as this. I am always ready to meet my hon. friends opposite in any constructive suggestions looking to the welfare of this country, but up to the present we have had nothing of the kind from that side of the house. I do not complain about that. It was the idea of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that the session should be adjourned instead of being prorogued, as I suggested. He won his point, and we are meeting here again at this time. Of course speeches are necessary, and many have been delivered by high ranking orators on the other side. But, Mr. Chairman, is it not possible for hon. gentlemen opposite to cease

The War-Mr. Pouliot

their insinuations and propaganda about leadership? We have a leader. He is the Prime Minister of Canada, who has headed the government of this country for perhaps longer than any other man in our history, including Sir John A. Macdonald. He has had remarkable success, and while I do not agree with everything that is done by the government I find that on the whole the Liberal party is alive while the Conservative party is dead. That is the principal difference.
Now that the Conservative party is to have a new leader I am reminded of the story of a king of Portugal named Pedro, who had a sweetheart called Inez de Castro. She was a very beautiful woman, but fell ill and died a long time before King Pedro was crowned. But at the time of his coronation he had her embalmed body mounted on a horse and paraded through the streets of Lisbon. That is the sort of parade we will have when Right Hon. Arthur Meighen becomes leader of the Conservative party; he will be parading with a corpse.
I believe we are coming to the time when there will be reciprocity between the parties, with a mutual exchange not of prisoners but of members.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I understand it my hon. friend is chivalrously speaking on my behalf, so perhaps my motive will not be mistaken if I intervene at this stage to say just a word to the committee. In my position as leader of the house I have a duty which the country will expect me to perform; it is to see to it that as far as possible the house conducts its proceedings in a manner worthy of the House of Commons, taking into account the very serious situation which exists in the world at the present time.
Through the leaders of the different parties and groups, all hon. members have agreed upon a certain procedure while the house is in committee. The purpose of the house sitting in committee was to afford every possible opportunity to hon. gentlemen on all sides to question the ministry with respect to Canada's war effort. I have been listening to the speeches this afternoon. Last night I was not in the house, because during the course of the evening I had to give consideration to some very important matters, but I have glanced over Hansard, and I must say it does not appear that many questions were directed to the minister, bearing directly on the affairs of his department, which he was here to discuss with hon. members.
I am in this difficult and embarrassing position, that the moment I suggest it would be well for hon. members to follow the order that has been agreed upon, and to refrain fMr. Pouliot.]
from making irrelevant speeches, I am immediately charged with trying to shut off discussion, and trying to prevent freedom of speech in the House of Commons. Notwithstanding, having heard so many speeches entirely irrelevant to the matters directly under discussion, I believe the government will have to conclude that hon. members have finished with that portion of the proceedings relating to the questioning of the ministers, and have reached the point where all hon. members will be free to speak on anything they wish in regard to public affairs. I was careful to say that in the latter part of the discussion time would be especially reserved, after the ministry had reported on the war effort and questions had been asked; that when an hon. member wished to speak on other matters ample opportunity would be given to do so. If at this stage hon. members are going to continue to speak on subjects wholly apart from departmental statements, then there is nothing for the government to do but to assume that we have reached a point where at least for the time being hon. members generally feel that the specific questioning of ministers is over.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that while it is understood by all that you should not seek to be other than generous in the way of giving hon. members the fullest possible latitude in matters of discussion, at this stage of the proceedings at any rate you should see to it that hon. gentlemen are reminded that the discussion should relate primarily to the department whose minister has his statement before the house at the moment. The Minister of Munitions and Supply has been here for some time. He has very important matters to which he must give attention. Now he has left, believing the committee are finished with him. At the moment the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services is here and we are ready to proceed with his department. I would ask hon. members please to join with the government in helping to expedite this part of the proceedings by reserving such general statements as they may wish to make until a later stage of the proceedings.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The procedure has been unusual from the beginning of this discussion, but by unanimous consent a rule has been established, as set out by the Prime Minister; and that rule is as binding on us in the course of this debate as any other rule under the standing orders of the house. Therefore I shall, in directing debate in the committee, adhere to the direction which has just been given and which, I understand, received the general assent of the committee.

The War-Mr. White

I merely wish to be quite clear upon the point. There are certain things about which I wish to speak. I wish to deal with the foreign policy of the government, and would relate my remarks to numbers of departments. But if I understand the Prime Minister to say that private members will have an opportunity to speak later on matters of general interest, then I shall be most pleased now to do as the Prime Minister suggests, and wait until the various ministers have been before the committee. Is that the understanding?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Quite correct.
May I have some idea in what order the ministers will be asked their questions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are here now.
Other ministers will follow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Other ministers are waiting, and will be prepared to answer questions in the order in which they made their respective 'statements.
The Minister of National Defence will come too?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope the Minister of National Defence may be able to be in the house to-morrow. He has for the last two days been confined to his house with a cold, and I think very wisely has sought to run no risk at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), and I wish to take the strongest exception possible to the remarks which he made when he alluded to Canadian soldiers overseas as young fools. I submit that no one in Canada, least of all-
Not all of them.

Please do not interrupt. I say that no one in Canada, least of all an hon. member in this chamber, has any right to refer to any member of the Canadian forces wearing the king's uniform, and serving in England, as a young fool. I would ask the hon. member for Temiscouata if he has ever worn the king's uniform, or rendered any service to his king. What right has he to speak?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The form of the hon. member's speech is not according to the ndes. He cannot ask a question as in a cross-examination in court. I suggest the hon. member should make his statement, or his speech, without putting questions to hon. members who have not the floor.

Thank you. But the circumstances are very exceptional. The hon. member for Temiscouata also referred to intrigues by Tory officers in the army. I would remind hon. members that all officers who serve in the army are subject to the strictest military discipline, and they are not permitted or allowed in any way to reply to charges against them.
On the day of the opening of the house 1 heard over the radio an announcement to the effect that the speech to be delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the beginning of the session would 'be the most important announcement made since the war started. Yet when I read his speech in Hansard I find no information as to what he saw or heard on his trip to England. Neither did I-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I say a word with regard to this matter. In the first place I do not think I am responsible for anything that is said over the radio. In the second place the speech I made at the opening of the house did not purport to be anything other than a statement of the international situation. I have made such statements each time when the house has reassembled, either at the beginning of a session or after an adjournment, and I was following that procedure. Similarly, on occasions when the house has met, either at a new session or after adjournment, after I have made such a statement the leader of the opposition has been the first to speak. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) expressed to me his desire to speak following my statement on the international situation. My hon. friend made his speech, and it was arranged by agreement that we would then follow the usual method with regard to other leaders in the house making their addresses. But what I myself said was nothing more, and purported to be nothing more than a statement on the international situation. As Prime Minister, if I have any statement of national policy to make I will not choose the end of the session to make it, but I will make it at the time of the session when it can be debated in the regular way, and when, in accordance with the rules, amendments can be made to any motion which may be based upon it.

.1 realize fully what the Prime Minister has said. But at the same time, as Prime Minister of this country, when he visited England, and was in consultation with the most important men in the world to-day, he saw with his own eyes what was
14873-269J
The War-Mr. White

going on. He was told, or must have been told, what we needed to do in this country. Surely, then, this parliament would have the right to expect, or would have the right to hear at the earliest possible moment, a review or report from the Prime Minister. If he chooses to wait, it is quite within his own power to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not choose to wait, even for parliament to meet. I made a broadcast to the country within a week or ten days after I returned, and that broadcast has been distributed to all members of parliament, and pretty generally throughout the country. I went very fully into the matters I regarded as most important in connection with my visit overseas.
If the house expects to hear from me the confidential discussions which took place between the Prime Minister of England and myself, and between other British cabinet ministers and myself, or between myself and those who have to do with matters of military strategy, then I am afraid I shall have to disappoint hon. members in that regard, because I do not regard my conferences overseas as intended to serve any such purpose. Unfortunately I cannot make public what it is necessary to conceal from the enemy.
I should like to make perfectly clear that I have not had the opportunity since I came back to discuss with some of my colleagues to the extent I should like, some of the matters which were taken up overseas. The Minister of National Defence, as hon. members know, left for the old country almost immediately after the time I came back. I have not had the opportunity to discuss with him, nor have my colleagues, the results of some of his conferences on the other side. And until we have that opportunity I do not propose on behalf of the government to make any premature statement with respect to what further step we will take as a result of our conferences.

Certainly I would not even suggest to the Prime Minister that he should discuss any of the confidential conferences which took place. But I do say that this house is entitled at least to a report and a true picture of the present situation overseas, and what is expected from Canada which, the Prime Minister says, is going to make a total war effort. Surely, then, the Prime Minister can tell us, after being over there, what is expected, and how Canada is to make a total war effort.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not need to go overseas to tell that. I told the house that at the beginning of the session, and I

have told it time and again in the speeches I have made. Everything I saw in England and heard in England, and everything said in conference in England confirmed what I had said were my convictions respecting the war, and as to Canada's part in the war, and above all caused me to feel an even greater pride in Canada's war effort than would have been possible if I had not been over there.
Would the Prime Minister care to say if in his opinion to-day Canada is making a total war effort?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say Canada is making a magnificent effort, and that everything considered, compared with the effort of any other country it will compare favourably. I will say to my hon. friend, when he speaks of total war effort, that I do not mean that the war effort of Canada is to be only in one direction-and that in the direction that is going to cause, in the matter of public discussion in this country, the most by way of embarrassment.

The Prime Minister apparently refers to the question of man-power. We heard the other day from the Minister of National Defence that the matter of manpower was most urgent and important. He admitted that we were not obtaining to-day, on the voluntary system of enlistment, the required number of recruits. He also admitted that the government quotas were not being obtained. I am informed that in some military districts the number of discharges on some days exceeds the number of enlistments. Perhaps when the minister is in his seat again he will tell us if that information is correct.
No doubt voluntary enlistment has produced many men, but in my opinion this form of enlistment is not sufficient. I have said before in this house, and I repeat, that selective compulsory military training is the only method that will meet the present emergency. At times in this house and out of the house and in the newspapers we hear and see the phrase, "equality of service and sacrifice." Is there any member of this house who will differ with me when I say that the only people of Canada who are making a sacrifice to-day are the men who are serving the empire for $1.30 a day? Do hon. members believe that the young men who stay at home and are in receipt of increased wages, who have the best of meals and all the comforts of civilized life, are making the same sacrifice as the boys in the armed forces? I repeat that the only men who are making a sacrifice to-day are those who are getting SI .30 a day. Yet this government

The War-Mr. White
passed regulations providing for a cost of living bonus to be paid to many thousands of Canadian citizens.
It is true that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated a few days ago that the question of increased allowances for soldiers' dependents was being considered, but these allowances apply only to three dependents-the wife and two children. These allowances were set, probably on some proper scale, in August and September of 1939, but according to the figures of the government the cost of living has increased by some 14 to 15 per cent. In the important essentials of life I think everyone will agree that the increase has been more than that, probably between 20 and 25 per cent. Surely a country that can raise billions of dollars for war can provide proper allowances for soldiers' dependents. In the Globe and Mail of to-day appears a report of an interview between a number of ladies and the Minister of Finance. The minister is reported to have said:
The man who enlists makes a sacrifice, and I am asking whether it is ever possible to make up in money the difference between the man who goes and the man who stays at home.
Later on the minister is reported to have asked:
The question is, can the country pay it?
Surely the Minister of Finance does not question the ability of this country to provide properly for the dependents of our soldiers overseas. The adoption of some system of selective compulsory training would have the effect of placing every man and woman of Canada where he or she could serve best in a total war effort. Until such a method is adopted I submit that we are not making anything like a total war effort. The time for this is not to-morrow or next week or next session; it is right now. I sincerely hope that this house will not be permitted to adjourn without some announcement being made by the Prime Minister. I hope we shall be told how Canada is going to make a total war effort and how the necessary man-power will be secured.
Speaking a few days ago in this house, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said that the responsibility for obtaining men for the army rested upon the members of this house and the people whom they represented in the constituencies. I disagree with that ' statement. The responsibility for obtaining the necessary men rests upon the shoulders of the Minister of National Defence and upon the shoulders of the government which he represents.
The Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) dealt in detail with certain regulations which had been passed by his department. He referred to the fact that a recruit could be examined by any doctor he wished, and he said also that there had been a large number of rejections. I should like to ask him if any further examination is made besides the first one, and whether or not any complaints have been made about this method. One hears various stories about the methods which have been adopted in some training centres to induce men to enlist for active service, often referred to as press-gang methods. As long as it is felt that there should be only voluntary enlistments, the method of inducing men to enlist which has been adopted in certain training centres should be stopped.
These are probably the most important regulations which have been passed in years, and yet they were passed by order in council. They affect several hundred thousand young men, and yet they were not considered of sufficient importance to be brought into this house for debate. The minister made it quite clear that there were no total exemptions. I should like to draw to his attention, as I have done before, the fact that many young farmers have been called up, in many cases only sons. The government have been urging increased production of bacon and other farm products, and yet in many cases they take away the only help left available to the farmer. Many farmers are reducing the number of cattle, sheep and hogs on their farms and cutting down in other production. Only ten days ago I was in a small country store in the township of Rawdon, one of the largest cheese-producing centres in eastern Ontario. I found seven farm sale bills. Upon inquiry I found that in every case the farmer was disposing of all his stock and assets because he could get no help. Some of these men had sons who have been called for service, while others had found that they could not compete with the prices paid for labour in the industrial centres.
I suggest to the Minister of National Services that he try to work out some scheme whereby young farmers and the only sons of farmers should be granted some form of exemption. If I understoood the minister correctly, he stated that such men could apply for exemption or an extension up to six months, and then at the end of that period a second exemption could be applied for but that that ended it. A farmer must plan ahead the same as anyone else. Many farmers have pointed out to me that if they are going to
The War-Mr. White

lose their help next summer they want to know ahead of time in order that they may reduce their stock and make other necessary arrangements.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. gentleman and the committee that the special rules established for this debate are that we should debate the statement of the minister which is at the moment before the committee. The statement now before the committee is that of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald). It will be very difficult for the chair to carry out the instructions of the committee if hon. members do not cooperate and confine their remarks to the department whose affairs are now before the committee. In discussing the affairs of the Department of National War Services the hon. member is anticipating, because the statement of the minister of that department will come before the committee after it has finished with the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. I shall certainly try to be broad in my rulings, but I am afraid that the hon. gentleman is going beyond what is reasonable.

I understood the Prime
Minister to say that the Minister of National War Services was here in addition to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes; but the business
before the committee now is the statement of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. After that we shall take up the affairs of the Department of National War Services.
I want to ask one question.

If I can have just a moment I will finish, and defer the further remarks I wish to make regarding matters which pertain to the Department of National War Services. I wish just to refer to the little blue pamphlet issued by the department in which there is a brief quotation which applies to the 11th of November; it is from the immortal poem of John McCrae:
Take up our quarrel with the foe!
To you from failing hands we throw The torch-be yours to hold it high!
This is Armistice day, and I would remind hon. members that those two words "to you" apply to every one of us. That is the challenge from the comrades who sleep in Flanders fields. I hope and trust that we shall not fail them.

I should
like to ask the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services what is the position with respect to over-recruiting for the navy. Representations have been made to me that in the city of Halifax alone are 2,000 recruits who have not been called for duty; they have been termed by some people-not by me-"the penguins"; they sit and wait. Perhaps the minister has heard that term. It is evident, I think, from the information which comes to hand that there has been over-recruiting for the navy having regard to the facilities available for their training and to their usefulness on the seas. What is the position with respect to the whole situation, not only that in the city of Halifax, which I assume is the centre of the greatest naval activities, but elsewhere in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A distinction, I think, must be made between the number of men who apply to serve in the navy and the number of those who are actually enrolled. When I said the other day that there were 4,000 men on the waiting list, I meant men who had not yet joined the navy but who had expressed willingness to join and whose applications to that effect were on file in the department. So far as I know at this time, there is no such condition as my hon. friend has heard of, in the city of Halifax or elsewhere. There are no 2,000 men there who should be at sea and who are not at sea. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition and my hon. friend the member for Yale will understand what is the situation. A very considerable number of men is required at bases established on shore-a number at least equal to the number afloat; and in Halifax, Esquimalt and other cities we have a considerable number of men ashore, but that by no means implies that they are doing nothing, that their time is wasted. I shall be glad to look further into the matter, but at this time, so far as I know, there are no such conditions as those to which my hon. friend referred.

I did not quite follow the minister's answer, because it seems to me to imply that there are none waiting to get into
the service-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, yes.
-but there are those in the service now who are being employed on shore.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No. It is the reverse. There are, as I said the other day, 4,000 waiting to get into the service.

The War-Naval Services
They are as yet in civilian life, but their applications are on file, and I assume that most of them would be available if called upon. They are those who have written in at one time or another expressing a desire to join the navy. That is the waiting list.
As to the men on shore, of course there are men on shore-there always will be-for the navy, a number at least equal to the number at sea. Reinforcements are needed, and the depots must be kept up. But to say that there are 2,000 in Halifax who are more or less wasting time, idling, is to say what is not so. There are a number in training there. Some of them will go to sea shortly. But I know of no case where time is being wasted and men are merely loafing.

Then, what will the policy be with regard to these youngsters who for several years past have had their eye on sea service, and are anxious to enter that service when they attain the proper age? Will they be given any sort of preferred consideration, or will they have to wait until this two, three, or four thousand waiting list has been disposed of?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The class to which my hon. friend refers is a very desirable class for the navy. It is known that those young men who have been training as boys in such organizations as the sea cadets are able to take their places in the navy with less training than men who have had no such experience. I should say that those who belonged to the sea cadet corps in one part of the country or another have an excellent chance of getting into the navy. They are all young and keen, and their services can be put to use more quickly on account of their training.
When I gave the figure of 4,000, my hon. friend will understand, of course, that some of those are probably unfit; some may be a little over-age, but that js the number of applications on file in the department.
Would the minister indicate in a general way how many are being taken on per month in the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In the last year the number has run at the rate of something over 1,000 per month. It varies from month to month, but that is about the average since November last.

To go back to the question of these chaps who have expressed their desire to enlist in the navy; in the district which I represent there is a considerable number, included in that 4,000, who want to
join the navy, and it has been necessary to tell them, and they have been told, that for some months at least there is no prospect of their being able to get in on the quota for that particular station. Is it a matter of policy to encourage those young men who are among the more desirable to become recruits in another branch of the service, and not to wait until next April or whenever they are likely to be called upon to join the naval services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would be asking a great deal of me to ask that I should urge the most desirable class of recruits to join other branches of the service. I have not done that. I do not know whether the Minister of National Defence, or the Minister of National Defence for Air has endeavoured to attract these men. I have no doubt men have joined other services because they are afraid it would be too long before they could get into the navy.
May I take it that the men on the waiting list whose applications have been received are awaiting entry into the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is the great feeding ground for the navy now. It is difficult to say exactly what the percentage is, but by far the overwhelming majority of those who come into the navy come in through the volunteer reserve divisions. They are really now the back-bone of the recruiting system.

That being the situation, there may be a different category. There is the old category of boys attaining a certain age and entering the Royal Canadian Navy itself, not via the volunteer reserve. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Is there such a category now?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are not taking boys into the Royal Canadian Navy now.
What is the minimum age at which they will be accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Eighteen.

Following on the suggestion of the minister about the preferment that might be given sea cadets who had training, boys who had received training for three or four years in sea cadet corps, are these young men, as they become eighteen, given
The War-Naval Services

preferment over those who have had no training and no inclination for such training up to the present time, or must they take their place definitely with the others?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a difficult question. I should say that in recruiting, if there were twenty-five candidates before a recruiting officer, five of whom he knew to be excellent material, he would take those five first if he could. That is almost inevitably the course that would be followed.
That is the policy outlined by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, it is not outlined. No policy has been outlined of giving preferment to anyone, but recruiting officers take the best men available.

I do not wish to pursue this point very far, but in my district there is an active sea cadet corps and we have young men who have grown up in that sort of work. We have had one of the greatest developments there in the past few months, thanks to one of the service clubs and other public-spirited citizens. We have a great many groups of young men who have been in training for three, four and five years. There seems to be a feeling that they have to mark time and take their place with the others just as if they had never had the advantage of this training. That is the point I want to have definitely cleared up, so that these young men will feel that their training is not lost, and that they will not have to take the usual place in line with those who desire to enlist in the Royal Canadian Navy. I am anxious to have that point cleared up. Will the minister indicate whether these boys will have preferment, having attained the age of eighteen, if they wish to offer their services? Are they not given some preferment as a matter of policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is not a matter of policy in the department to give preferment to anyone, but I put this to my hon. friend. If he were recruiting and he had the opportunity to take twenty men of the type he has been describing or twenty men who were absolutely green, he would undoubtedly take the twenty who had training.
I presume the naval recruiting officers will do the same. These men can be made ready for the sea more quickly than the others, and there are some things that they know already; consequently it is desirable to take them, and that is the practice. But it would be a great mistake for the department to order that a certain class or group should be given priority or preferment as a matter of right. That would be a mistake and it has not been done, 
though in practice I have no doubt that what my hon. friend says does happen. He will understand, of course, that recruiting for the Canadian navy is now done chiefly through these volunteer reserve divisions which are in eighteen different parts of Canada. If a sea cadet corps is not near a division, the boys may have a little problem in that way. If the sea cadet corps the hon. member has in mind is not so situated, there may be some difficulty on that account. The boys have to go to the nearest volunteer reserve division to enlist, and that might put them to some inconvenience. But we cannot undertake at this time to establish any more volunteer reserve divisions because we are short of the trained officers to command them.

I quite agree with the minister that he can hardly give preference to sea cadets. I know from my own experience that in the maritime provinces there are a great many young men who have spent their whole lives on the sea. While they have not had an opportunity of training as sea cadets, they have had very practical training on the sea, and these men do wish to get into the navy. Unfortunately, in recruiting, we have had to turn them down recently, and it has been a great disappointment to men on the southern coast of New Brunswick and along the Northumberland straits, as well as in other parts where they have followed the sea all their lives. The men in our part of Canada seem to have a great desire to enlist in the navy, and it is unfortunate that we cannot take more men of that type. They prefer it to the infantry, the air force or other services.
Will the minister answer a question with regard to the Royal Naval college? He mentioned the other day that the college would be opened in the fall of 1942. I should like him to explain the method of selecting students for this college, the age, and whether they will be selected proportionately throughout Canada -I mean whether there will be a quota for each province the same as for the Royal Military college at Kingston. He might also tell us the number they propose to train at the college when it opens in the fall of 1942.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am glad to give that information. For the naval college the number of students will be 100. The method of selection will be somewhat the same as in the Royal Military college, namely, by provinces. As far as possible we shall try -to give cadetships in proportion to the number from the particular province who apply. That seems to be the fairest way of doing it. As regards the other conditions of entry, educational qualifications and so on, broadly speaking, the boy must have junior

The War-Naval Services
matriculation at least. There will be one-year courses for the older boys and two years for the younger. The prospectus will be issued shortly setting forth all these details.

In connection with the
