preferment mentioned by the hon. member, I never agreed with the policy of trying to get a large number of men in the navy or naval forces who are inland men and have never seen a tide or high or low water. If preference is given to those men simply because they are in thickly-populated centres where they can form into groups, whether of sea cadets or otherwise, thus setting back men who have lived all their lives by the sea and know the things peculiar to the sea, it would be doing a great injustice. I have always thought there should be more facilities for taking advantage of the experience of young men who have lived all their lives on the seashore. There are some things that they do not have to learn. It is a misfortune that we have not some organization which would enable groups of such men even in small centres to be trained in the same way that they are trained in central Canada. We are not making the best use of the valuable material available on our coasts. I do not want to discourage enlistment in the army, but we have men in the army who have lived all their lives by the sea, and it is a pity 6ome system is not worked out to make the best use of their experience.

I just want this clarified. The impression is abroad among these young men that they just had to take their course and they had some preference. I rather agree that young men living by the sea are good material for the naval services.

Apparently Canada will soon be faced with the necessity of recruiting several thousand men for the merchant marine because a hundred cargo ships are to be completed next year. What plans have been made for recruiting these merchant seamen and what training will be given them, also what rates of pay, and will they be eligible for pension? I do not think it is possible to raise this number of men in a hurry; plans will have to be made quite a while before the men are called for. There should be something under way now in that connection.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is a question which perhaps my hon. friend should direct to the acting Minister of Transport. I think the minister made some reference to that point the other night and indicated that a maiming station is to be established where merchant seamen would be
trained. The Department of Naval Services is not directly concerned with that problem, but has on many occasions discussed it with the Department of Transport and volunteered to do anything asked by way of assisting in or supervising the training, in gunnery, for example, and that sort of thing, of these merchant seamen. That is purely voluntary on our part.

I asked the Minister of
Munitions and Supply last night, and he said it was a matter for the Minister of Transport and the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. Surely some one should know something about this policy. On page 4093 of Hansard the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs is reported as saying:
The protection of merchant shipping is one of our tasks, but the provision of merchant ships and of merchant seamen is in other hands. The Canadian naval staff, however, have taken a deep interest in the training and supply of merchant seamen and have cooperated with the Department of Transport in the provision of manning pools in this country, where merchant seamen may register and remain while awaiting employment on a merchant ship.
Surely someone in the ministry can give more information about these plans, if there are any. It may be that it is still just talk.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The statement read by my hon. friend bears out what I said to-day. We are to protect merchant shipping by escort vessels, yes, but we are not charged with the duty of providing seamen or ships. I did go on to say that we have taken an interest in the matter through some of our officers. We have cooperated with the Department of Transport in establishing manning pools and drawing up schemes for the training of merchant seamen, but that, as I say, is a purely voluntary effort on our part. My department has nothing to do with providing merchant seamen, that is for the Department of Transport. I think the remarks of the acting Minister of Transport last night cleared up the question the hon. member has in mind.

The Minister of Munitions
and Supply said, as reported on page 4223 of II ansard:
The Department of Transport has taken in hand the task of training crews for merchant ships. Manning pools have been established at Halifax and Montreal and are now in operation. Training schools are also being built in connection with these manning pools. It is the intention to pursue an intensive programme of enlisting and training candidates for the merchant marine.
It may be that is as far as the matter has gone. But the committee should be told whether that is the situation, or if the plans have been developed further we should know.
The War-Naval Services

For example, are young men to be recruited for the merchant marine, or will they be older men not eligible for the navy or the other fighting forces? Must they be in A category, and will arrangements be made to protect their wives and children? All these details should be given at as early a date as possible so that right across the country men who are interested in the merchant marine may be able to make plans to enlist; otherwise we may find ourselves with a lot of ships and no one to man them.

The manning pool is something more than my hon. friend suggests, merely a place for seamen to register. It is a place where seamen can really sign on for service and go on pay. A ship discharges a crew on this side. These men can immediately go to the manning pool, be provided with housing, if they stay in port, and remain on pay until such time as they are assigned to another ship. Similarly any Canadian can register at the manning pool. If he requires training; if he is not up to the standard required for merchant ships, there is a school which will give him that training, and of course throughout the period he is on pay.
As acting minister I have not the intimate knowledge of the situation that perhaps I should have, but I shall be very glad to consult with my deputy and give my hon. friend any further information that may be available. We have an organization in charge of exceptionally well qualified men, and we believe that the manning pools and the schools for merchant seamen will make a real contribution.

I suggest that these manning pools should be opened in other parts of the country. Apparently at the present time there is one in Montreal and one in Halifax. I think there should be one or perhaps two on the west coast.
I believe that is contemplated.
It may be that there should also be manning pools at the great lakes ports. How many men make up the crew of one of these 10,000-ton merchant ships?

When I was in charge of the Department of Transport I was well versed in these matters, but since I have been devoting my attention to the Department of Munitions and Supply I have forgotten many of the details. I would not attempt to give information of that sort, which might not be reliable. I will, however, obtain a memo on the whole subject and be prepared to give the information later in the session.

What
provision is being made for the training of navigating officers? I think the minister will find a great dearth of these men.

I should think the school would certainly give instruction of that kind, leading to officer's papers; but, as I say, I should prefer not to go into detail with regard to these schools until I find out more about them.

Then I should like to ask the navy minister a question having to do with rates of pay of men in the navy. My understanding is that men in the navy receive less pay than men in the other fighting forces. That understanding may be incorrect, but if it is correct perhaps the minister will tell us why that should be the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, that is not correct, to answer the question generally. There is some difference, which has existed for a long time, between certain ranks in the navy and corresponding ranks in the army, but to say that generally men in the navy are paid less than the others is not correct. One may be able to take one rank in the navy and find some difference when one compares it with the corresponding rank in the army or air force, but as a general rule the pay runs about the same.

Will the minister mention the ranks in which there is a difference? I understand, for instance, that there is a difference between the pay of a lieutenant in the army and the pay of a naval officer holding equivalent rank, and it may be the same as between non-commissioned officers in the army and petty officers in the navy. Is there any reason for this situation? Are we simply following an old British custom instead of paying men on a Canadian basis? If so, it does not seem the fair thing to do.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think this question was discussed in the house at considerable length last session. At that time I stated that when it is said that a man in the navy is paid so much a day, it must be remembered that in many instances there is some extra pay. There is hard-lying money, and there are various other extras which the men in the navy may receive. Until recently sublieutenants in the navy were receiving less than lieutenants in the army, which would be the corresponding rank. That situation has been rectified, however, within recent months, so that now a sublieutenant in the navy receives the same pay as a lieutenant in the army. I cannot undertake, at the moment, to give my hon. friend a

The War-Naval Services
comparison between all ranks in the three services. I have that information, but it is not here. I can get it and table it to-morrow.
Is there any reason why they should not be all on the same basis?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is the one reason which I just mentioned, namely, that in the navy there are little odds and ends that are sometimes tacked on to a man's pay, or even an officer's pay, which may make the total emolument equal to that received by a man in the army or the air force. It is true that if one considers the basic pay, $4 or $5 a day, he may think there is a difference; but when one works it out, he finds that it is pretty generally the same. I admit that there are some differences. Some men in the navy get a little more than those holding corresponding ranks in the army, while some get a little less.
I raised the question because I know there has been a certain amount of discontent by reason of that fact, and I think the situation should be rectified as far as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The whole question is being inquired into now by an interservice committee on pay. I agree with my hon. friend that perhaps some of these extras which are allowed in one way or another should be dispensed with and that there should be a uniform rate of pay for similar ranks in all three services. As I say, that question is being studied by a committee. In the meantime I have tried to rectify some cases in the navy where I thought increases were justified, and the case of the sublieutenant was one of these.

We were pleased to hear of the expansion of the navy, as outlined by the minister the other day. I think at that time he said the personnel had been increased to 27,000 officers and men. We know that increase has been brought about over a very short period of time, and I should like to ask hovr the navy has been able to train officers to take charge of so many vessels and such a large number of men, whether we have been able to do it all here in Canada or -whether we have had to bring in officers from elsewhere. In the army we know there were a great many militia units with trained officers, so that it was easy to expand the army; but for the navy to expand so quickly and still have competent officers seems to me to be something phenomenal, as the minister has said, unless some of these officers were brought from somewhere outside Canada, because we had so little in the way of training facilities in this dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Of course for the last fifteen or seventeen years we did have a naval militia, the volunteer naval reserve, which in a sense would correspond with the army militia. They trained at certain times, and they were of great value when war came and the demand for officers and petty officers became so pressing. Apart from that, and other Canadian sources, we have not relied on any other quarter for our officers and petty officers. I think within the last year we may have had from England one or two officers with very special training of one kind or another; I do not think there were more than perhaps two. The rest have come from our own ranks. While it has been difficult to train officers and petty officers of that kind, it must be remembered that these men who are now undertaking training receive, in perhaps one year, the training which in peace time would require three or four years. They gain by experience which, in peace time, would require years and years to acquire.
We try to break them in with experienced officers. There is splendid material in the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, which includes those men who have come up from the merchant shipping lines. These are men who are skilled at sea. The same problem is being faced in the old country. They have expanded their navy, and they have had to hurry up their training as best they could, and entrust young men with heavy responsibilities. But there is no other way it can be done.
Will the naval college be located in the east, the west, or the middle?
Possibly up at Churchill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is almost certain that the college will be located in the west. That is the opinion of the experts who have studied the question. Climatic conditions out there, the possibility of doing sea work at all times of the year, make the west more desirable in their opinion.
We do not want fair-weather sailors; we want men who can take it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In the opinion of the naval officers it is easier to train men at the west coast in the winter months. It is colder in the east, and that fact offers some difficulty when men are asked to get out in open boats to do boat work in December, January and February. The weather is more favourable on the Pacific coast. For these reasons we believe better training can be given on the west coast during the college term.

About a year ago the government announced that it was planning to build destroyers and light cruisers in Canada. The other day the minister said wTe were about to
The War-Naval Services

begin the construction of destroyers. Has the plan for building light cruisers been given up, or are we to build them eventually?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not believe I ever made any announcement about light cruisers. Certainly they will not be built in the immediate future. At the moment there is no plan to build such craft in this country. The plans for building destroyers are well in hand, and we hope to begin that work very soon. This time it will be done on the east coast, at Halifax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that this concludes the debate on the statement by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services?
It concludes the questioning, unless someone else wishes to speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then the Department of National War Services will be before the committee.
If I may have permission I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) some questions which should have been asked earlier in the afternoon.
I have no objection.

I refer particularly to the minister's remarks respecting aircraft production. At page 4082 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
Our aircraft industry has manufactured in Canada and placed in service since the outbreak of war, or has assembled in Canada, 3,749 aircraft.
How many of those aircraft were actually manufactured in Canada? Then, has aircraft production in Canada met the expectations expressed by him to the committee in March and April last?

I have not the break-down as between planes manufactured in Canada and those assembled here, but I shall obtain that information. As to expectations-yes, I believe all our plants are manufacturing pretty well to the output we anticipated. The programme has been changed to some extent in that there has been a definite move toward larger planes, and away from trainer and operational planes. Therefore the numbers may be out a bit. Certainly, however, from the point of view of man-hours and output I believe our programme is all we ever intended it to be.

How is the manufacture of parts proceeding, as far as elementary training planes are concerned? During

the past summer the committee on national war expenditures visited the various elementary flying training schools in eastern Canada. Generally speaking, one of the chief complaints made by those operating the schools had to do with the failure on the part of the aircraft industry to supply the necessary parts. Almost without exception we were advised in the training schools that for periods of two or three months at a stretch often as - many as 20 per cent of the number of planes allotted to a particular school could not be put into the air by reason of the failure of Federal Aircraft. It was criticized, in certain instances. Then there was mention of failure by some of the private manufacturers to supply parts.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Is my hon. friend talking about elementary schools?
Yes.

Federal Aircraft is not
building anything for them.
I am wrong in that connection, as far as the elementary schools are concerned. The minister is right when he says that the parts do not come from them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are not for elementary schools, then?

That is correct; I should not have used the word "elementary". But, in so far as elementary schools are concerned, is it a fact to-day that planes are being kept on the ground on account of the failure of manufacturers to supply necessary parts or is that condition improving, and are the necessary parts being supplied as required?

I believe any country which must take care of vast fleets of aeroplanes find a difficulty with respect to parts. The difficulty is not so much that of having the parts in the country as it is that of having the right part at the right place when it is needed. There are standard lists of parts made. When aircraft are produced, about 20 per cent are made of spare parts, and these are stored at strategic points to take care of overhauls. The difficulty is that there can be no certainty as to whether a spare list will be correct for a certain area. It may be correct for the whole of Canada, but it often happens-in fact it happens regularly-that in a certain area there may be a run on spare parts of a certain type. When that condition arises we, of course, turn in and make more spare parts.
The greatest difficulty has come from the British type of planes which we received early in the war, and for which we did not receive an adequate supply of spare parts. Due to shipping losses, and due more particu-

The War-Munitions, and Supply
larly to the fact that it is only natural that one takes care of his own needs first, we have had difficulty in obtaining spare parts for those planes. The spare parts problem is just as acute in England as it is in Canada. We ordered very liberally of spare parts, and I think my colleague will agree with me when I say that the situation is better.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are some parts that cannot be made in Canada.

That is true. The British parts that cannot be made in Canada offer one great obstacle, but we are making certain British parts here to take care of some of the British planes that we have. We are gradually catching up with the situation. I may say that as long as we have the heavy overhaul programme that we have to-day there will be difficulty with spare parts. The problem in connection with spare engine parts is more difficult because the engines are not made in this country. But I do not think Federal Aircraft should be blamed. It is the British type of Anson that is giving us the trouble.
I heard that the aeroplane industry is progressing so rapidly in a scientific way that aeroplanes which were considered modern a year ago are obsolete to-day.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That would: apply largely to fighters, but not to trainers.

It does not apply to the class of aeroplane that we have been making or assembling in Canada. I can appreciate that that might be so in view of what I heard in the old country. I was wondering how it would have affected our own production if we had set up factories to make a certain type of aeroplane and then found it to be obsolete in a short time.

It all complicates the spare parts problem. We have four types of Anson aeroplanes, and each type requires certain spare parts. As one type goes out of production we must make ample provision for spare parts. The planes which were bought in the earlier stages now present an overhaul problem as, in some instances, spare parts have gone out of production. As I say, we have met this problem by organizing production in Canada

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We have had to replace
some of the older types of planes with a type which could be produced in Canada, even though they were more expensive.
Are we doing anything at all to get into the production of aeroplane engines?
No.

It seems to me that that is likely to become a bottleneck in the future. If all engines are produced in Great Britain and the United States, I think it ultimately will become a problem. Has any research work been done, or have any investigations been made by the department with a view to getting into the production of aeroplane engines?

That problem has been considered carefully. We inquired into the source of engines, both on this continent and in England, and an adequate supply was assured to us. It certainly would be more convenient if we could manufacture engines here, particularly in meeting the spare parts problem, but that cannot be done. Certain engines have become obsolete and we have a spare parts problem. The production of engines required by Canada would create a tremendous problem, and after a most exhaustive study it was decided that we had not the man-power or the machine-tool capacity to meet this problem in full.

It is a
tremendous problem in war time.

Terrific. Australia manufactures aeroplane engines in a small way, but we should bear in mind that Australia has never undertaken the production of automobile and truck engines as we have. It would be most difficult to undertake an intricate task of that kind and do it well, and we thought we would be well advised to leave this field to those countries that are better organized to undertake it.
Australia is so far away from sources of supply that she is practically forced to manufacture her own engines.
Yes.

The President of the United States has indicated that that country will have a production of 50,000 planes a year and they will take care of their own engine needs. After the war aviation in this country will certainly grow, and at some time or another Canada will have to get into the production of aeroplane engines. It is to be hoped that the government has some plan for the future production of our own aeroplane engines.

We must realize that after the war there will be engine capacity beyond all dreams of possible use. The engine capacity that is being created is tremendous. My hon. friend refers to the aeroplane production that is being planned in the United States, but I would tell him that engine production is
The War-War Services

being kept in step and our requirements are being considered in that programme. I think we may expect to have adequate supplies of engines during the war and a great glut of engine-making capacity after the war.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, the minister may remember that some months ago I drew his attention to the fact that Canadian news in south Africa did not seem to compare, in volume at least, with news from the other dominions. There are in the mining sections of south Africa a very large number of Canadians, and they are disappointed at listening so continually through the British Broadcasting Corporation, with messages emanating from Daventry, to descriptions of the war effort of the other dominions, and wonder what Canada has been doing. I drew the minister's attention to the matter at the time, and he told me that he would see what could be done with regard to it. Is he in a position now to describe further broadcasts of purely Canadian news in the other dominions?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
speechtext:
The subject of
building a shortwave broadcasting station has been receiving carefid consideration, but no decision in the matter has yet been arrived at. That will, perhaps, answer my hon. friend's question as to the point of broadcasting from this side.

Not entirely, because evidently the other dominions are able to make considerable use of Daventry; and I have always wondered why Canada should not place herself in the same position as, for instance, Australia and New Zealand with regard to news in south Africa.
We have not taken any steps in the direction of broadcasting Canadian information from Daventry.

But is the minister not prepared to do so? If Australia can do so, and if New Zealand can do so, surely, for the benefit of our Canadians in south Africa, it would be desirable to give them information with regard to what Canada is doing. Otherwise, these Canadians believe that Canada is slipping behind.

We have not done anything in that direction from the point of view of broadcasting. Of course, a number of copies of our other public information publications such as the one on Canada's war effort do go to south Africa. I would, however, be glad to give further consideration to the suggestion made by my hon friend.

To whom do these pamphlets go? As I have explained, these Canadians in south Africa are spread all over those very considerable areas where mining is the principal occupation; and it is inconceivable that these publications can be sent by post to such of those Canadians of whom the minister may be aware. Where they are in isolated situations-mining camps, mining towns and the like-it does tend rather to disgust them if they hear continuous descriptions of what other dominions are doing in this war effort, and they do not get their own Canadian news.
Probably there is the same situation in other parts of the empire. Have any steps been taken so that Australia, New Zealand and India may have some information as to what Canada is doing in the war?

The same method is in use. We do distribute to many portions of the globe leaflets giving particulars and facts relating to Canada's war effort, but we have not been broadcasting to the other dominions.
Would it not be possible to make some arrangement with the British Broadcasting Corporation so that at times such information would be given by them?
I replied to the hon. member for Yale that I would be glad to give further consideration to broadcasting from Daventry. If that is done, broadcasting can be arranged to all the dominions.

On this question, I should like to mention that African news comes over the German shortwave station, that is the 25-metre band, and we get it here quite plainly. They also have the 19, 20, 25, 31, 221 and 263 millimetre bands, over which they are broadcasting. Is anything being done in Canada to try to stop those shortwave broadcasts from coming here from Germany, because they do not say very nice things about Canada or the British empire?

How can we
stop them?

The
British government have stopped the Germans from broadcasting into England from their Norwegian stations. Is there not some method

The War-Mr. Picard
we can work out here, perhaps in conjunction with the United States government? This broadcast comes in during the morning from 10 to 10.30, and it is as clear as a bell; I am informed, in fact, that it is probably rebroadcast either in this country or in the United States.
I am not aware that Great Britain has stopped shortwave broadcasting from Germany-
From the northern part of Norway.
or from northern occupied countries. I hardly see how she could do that. I do not know how we could stop shortwave broadcasting from Germany or from German-occupied countries to this continent.
That station in Norway broadcast for some months before the British stopped it, but they have now, I understand, two stations in England interfering on it to stop it.
We have nothing of that sort in Canada.

That
particular matter was brought up in the British House of Commons.
We have nothing of that sort here.

On the subject of publicity generally, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister, and there are a couple of questions I wish to ask him.
The only way I know of to deal with information coming in such as we have been just discussing is to blot it out with a little broadcasting of our own. I am not particularly interested in the subject of shortwave radio broadcasting at the moment. I am interested in the dissemination of proper information about Canada's war effort, in Canada primarily, and then in the United States. It so happens that a large percentage of the Canadian people do not yet know, in spite of all that has been done, exactly what is going on; and certainly, if I may judge from the considerable numbers of United States citizens who pass through my own hands as recruits for the Canadian army, if one may assume that their knowledge is in any degree indicative of the general knowledge in the places from which they come, we are greatly mistaken if we imagine that much is known over there about our war effort.
I was encouraged by what the minister said the other day about the sending out of leaflets and pamphlets containing factual information,
but even that is not, I think, equal to the sort of top-flight reporting to which the United States public is accustomed. There is no doubt that our well-wishers in the United States are hungry for information about what we are doing, for two purposes-the encouragement it gives them in combating sentiment which is not friendly to us, and the inspiration it provides to their own people. I doubt whether the average United States citizen, any more than most Canadians, goes in much for either reading or listening to speeches, no matter how effective they are.
I might except the fireside chats of the president, though competent radio statisticians tell us that even he, who has perhaps the second largest radio audience in the world, does not begin to reach everybody. The minister might well consider encouraging those responsible for the dissemination of knowledge of our war effort to throw away their typewriters, give their voices a rest and invest in more cameras. We are a lazy people, accustomed to getting a good deal of information through our eyes. There is hardly a decent publication on the American continent that would not use a good picture, particularly if it could get it for nothing. The newsreaders have become accustomed to it, and I should like to know whether the minister would consider a wider use of pictorial news, particularly on the other side of the line.
I want to say a word with respect to the present utilization of quotas, but someone else may want to say something with regard to publicity and I will let that stand for the moment.

I do not intend to speak at any length or to analyse in detail the reports before the committee, one specific item relating to the question of publicity, about which my hon. friend has spoken, I should like to discuss, namely, the publicity given by the United States press to our war effort. I trust I may be permitted at this stage to make a few remarks on this subject.
On November 4 the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) spoke of "the importance of having Canada's war effort made more widely known in the United States than it is at the present time". Later on, in the course of the same day, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked for a "report on the work of the legation in Washington and what it had accomplished to counteract the sinister influence which has been depreciating Canada's war effort in the United States."
The War-Mr. Picard

If I may be allowed to be personal, I may say that I made it my duty, after the summer sessions of the war expenditures committee, to visit the United States, mainly Washington and New York, in order to acquaint myself better with the development of the defence programme there as well as with the opinion of our neighbours concerning the situation facing the world at large, and the grave decisions that will have to be taken by them at some time or another in the future.
It is not my intention to burden the committee with a recital of the conclusions I have reached on many important and interesting topics as a result of that trip. I reserve for some other day any observations I may wish to make as to the workings of the United States form of government as compared with ours, as well as the democratic control of government by the duly chosen representatives of the people even in time of war. Such more or less academic questions may just as well be treated later on, coupled with a study of the workings of our new extra-governmental set-up in the Department of Munitions and Supply, the Bank of Canada and its ramifications, and the other control agencies created since the war. I feel, however, it is my duty, since this question has been raised concerning one of the points I investigated while in the United States, to give the committee my humble opinion on the matter.
As to the publicity given our war effort by the United States press, I will admit that the impression I had after a few days in New York was that it was inadequate because it did not seem to reach the man in the street. I was astonished at the little that was known concerning what we were doing. It appeared to me, from this more or less elementary survey, that Canada's war effort was not only not front-page news but did not seem to have that news value there which we might have expected it to have. I must say, however, in all justice, that I have since then received a statistical survey by an agency dealing especially in inquiries of that sort, that reports that the United States press in July and August contained more items than appeared previously with regard to Canada, and that in September the condition was a little better. There is, however, still a lack of knowledge on the part of the public at large with respect to our contribution to the present conflict. Apart from the European war, apart from the far east question, the important international news which we find in the United States newspapers generally has to do with south American republics. Our cousins of the other America who were

never heard of in the United States press until a few years ago except when they overthrew a president are now front-page news, and Canada's main claim to fame for a large number of Americans is to have given its name to a ginger ale and supplied Madison Square Garden with hockey players.
Apart from some well-intentioned but not always outstanding articles on the question by some visiting reporters; apart from some articles by the representative of the New York Times in Ottawa; and apart from some of the more or less distorted reports by the rewrite men on the editorial staff of Time magazine, the only items of note which we find are reproductions of the criticism of our war effort as contained in the Tory Gazette and the Globe and Mail, and I do not think this is calculated to keep the people of New York well informed. I might also venture to say that while I was in New York some sort of exhibition was given which did not contribute to a fair understanding of our position. I am bound to say that it was given by the premier of Ontario in the course of speeches and statements during his last trip there. It is comforting, however, to see that in many other cities than New York editorials and reports have appeared about conditions in Canada giving a better impression and a better view of what is being done.
I have before me a report from the Cincinnati Inquirer of July 19, which states:
Every facet of the Canadian war effort is well planned and being well executed. Together, they constitute a splendid tribute to the courage, determination and ability of our friends across the border.
Later I came across an article that appeared in the Detroit Free Press in August, from which I quote:
Compared with our own war effort, Canada's is highly creditable. Stories to the contrary may have sprung from a misinterpretation of criticisms of the Canadian government's conduct of the war by certain Canadian newspapers.
I hasten to say that the situation as I found it in Washington was far different from that in New York. There I found government officials, members of the senate and of the house of representatives, generally well informed on all our doings, and the credit for that should be given to our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), because the persons more directly responsible for this better appreciation of Canada in Washington are working under his personal guidance. The first is our minister to the United States, Hon. Leighton McCarthy. I wish to take this opportunity to reassure any whom I have myself heard criticizing this appointment on

The War-Mr. Picard
the ground of the age of the appointee. I have seen our minister at work, and I wish to state that his keen mind, untiring energy and personal friendly connection of long standing with the president and many of his advisers, make him one of our most valuable assets and a contributing factor to a better understanding between our two countries. Also, while not overlooking the ability and usefulness of the staff of our legation, I wish to single out in connection with this matter of publicity the press attache who was selected four or five months ago and sent to Washington. I thought until a few minutes ago that he was under the ministry of information; I am now aware that he is directly under the Department of External Affairs. I may not be an expert in the matter, but when I compare the situation in Washington with that in New York and even between the New York press recently and in a period prior to the appointment of Mr. Reading, I would say his appointment was more than timely and seems to be proving a good one. This courteous, mild-mannered and apparently unassuming man seems already to have accomplished a good deal; his methods appear to have had a happier result in Washington than the blatant noises of more aggressive men.
Perhaps a different but just as efficient type of man might be needed by the ministry of information to handle the New York press boys if such an appointment were contemplated by the Prime Minister when he spoke in the house of the best possible methods being adopted by the Canadian government to supplement the actual sources of Canadian ' news in the United States. I have confidence that the Prime Minister as well as the ministry of information will deal with the New York situation and will bring about there as good results as have been achieved in Washington. May I emphasize at this time what the Prime Minister said in answer to the hon. member for Parkdale. He said that there is no "better means of making Canada's war effort known in the United States and elsewhere than to have our own press give a full appreciation of it," because most of the newspapers in the United States "obtain their information with respect to Canada's war effort from what appears in our own press."
When the leader of the opposition worries about the "sinister influences which have been depreciating Canada's war effort in the United States," he has only to think of some of his own friends, particularly of the Montreal Gazette and the Toronto Globe and Mail, because any criticism of the Canadian war
effort in the United States is not derived from opinion in the United States but is commented upon by that press as a result of the criticism seen in Canadian papers. Each outburst of unjustified criticism of the quality or extent of our participation is meat for the United States isolationists and their propagandists, and works ultimately against the interest of the British cause.
The same comment might apply to the harm done in this country by the unwarranted cries of the Tory press and Tory speakers concerning union government and other methods of carrying on the war. It appears evident that these apostles are not thereby so much helping the war effort of the country as furthering the political efforts of their party to blur the issues, alarm the country and divide the Liberals in order to gain power, or at least a share of it. I shall not at this moment discuss these questions because they are not so much in the public mind as the blatant noises of a few Tory newspapers and a boisterous minority would have us believe.

The hon. member has
learned his lesson in a good school.
I am glad of the compliment; I take it as such. The people of Canada have given a mandate to the present government to drive the car, and the Conservatives are thumbing to hitch-hike-
We do not want to hitchhike, but we want some decent driving.
They are not in the car and they already act like back-seat drivers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would remind hon. gentlemen that when the Chairman stands, hon. gentlemen should sit down, and furthermore when the Chairman is addressing the committee, hon. gentlemen should have respect for the Chair, if not for the Chairman. That makes for orderly discussion. The hon. member for Bellechasse has the floor.

Let him keep it on a
higher plane.

I must apologize to the
Chair; I evidently have not learned well enough yet from "that good school".
The people knew well what they were doing when they selected the present government in an election held more than six months after the beginning of the war.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member for Waterloo South to keep order.

I bow to your ruling.
The War-Mr. Picard

The people of Canada remembered when they chose this government, what kind of drivers they had during the last war, and they did not want to have the same experience again. They knew in what condition that cr"w left Canada after governing from 1911 to 1921, wrecking the unity and harmony of the country by a false interpretation of the nature of our participation in the war. When the people of Canada realize what has already been accomplished and what is in process of execution in the way of training as well as production; when they grasp the facts contained in the clear and frank statements of the ministers charged more directly'with the conduct of the war effort, they will know that Canada up to now has done more proportionately than any other country, except some of those in which the war has been waged actively.
It is imperative, however, that these facts be kept constantly before the public. The ministry of information has issued an illuminating booklet on the matter, but that is not enough; these facts should be repeated time and again so that our people may understand the magnitude of our accomplishment and derive from that the pride of duty well done. There is nothing for a Canadian to be ashamed of when a country with a population under 11,500,000 has already over 520,000 men under arms-

Oh, now, wait. Mr. Chairman, might I ask the hon. member a question? I think he should divide that 520,000 up as to where they are and what they constitute; otherwise we get a false impression throughout the whole country.

If my hon. friend will be patient, the division is coming in a moment. Of this number, 357,000 are enlisted for service overseas; 240,000 are in the active army, 90,000 are in the air force already blazing the skies with their exploits or in process of training, 27,000 are in the navy, convoying ships to Britain, patrolling our shores or getting ready to do so, and 170,000 are in our own territorial army manning the outposts of our home defences or training to play their part in the protection of their country.
Even the Liberals laugh at that.

There is nothing for a Canadian to be ashamed of when the industrial energy of his country has been geared in such a short time to make it one of the largest arsenals of the democracies, when its unending flow of munitions and war supplies is feeding the armies of our allies, when the

products of its agriculture are feeding the British isles. There is nothing for a Canadian to be ashamed of when this country is waging war to the tune of $4,000,000 daily, when it has lent to Britain in recent months nearly $1,000,000,000-

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. Just before the dinner recess the Chairman ruled that I must stop my speech and confine myself to asking questions. I ask what the hon. member is doing now? He is reading a speech right through.

On the point of order I wish to remind my hon. friend that I have dealt first with the question of publicity under the ministry of information, and I am now dealing with the question of man-power, which is under the Department of National War Services, because it is they who call to arms the territorial army. It is all relevant. At any rate I shall have finished in a moment.
Canada, true to its historical traditions, is doing its duty towards itself, towards its allies, and towards the sacred cause of liberty and democracy. It is doing it under the guidance of a trusted government, elected in time of war, especially for the conduct of the war, and it will continue doing it despite the intrigues and the alarming cries of the Tories.

Has the minister given attention to the questions which I directed to him during the course of his remarks, with respect to the medical examination of those called for training purposes, and the position with respect to the numbers examined?

When I spoke the other day the leader of the opposition and some other hon. gentlemen asked me a number of questions, some of which were repeated to-day by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterbor-ough. With regard to medical examinations, when a person receives notice that he is to be called up for training under the regulations he is notified to report for medical examination and may go to any doctor of his own choice. That is the first examination. That doctor is supposed to examine him in accordance with the standards that are set by the Department of National Defence.
Have all doctors those regulations, and do they know the requirements?
Yes.

They are all informed?

The War-War Services

Yes; they also receive a detailed examination form which they are required to complete, which form is sent in to the divisional registrar's office. Then there is a medical adviser attached to each administrative division, who can check these forms and the findings of the examining physician. If he feels there is any doubt about the category in which the man has been placed, he can order the man to report to any other doctor whom he may name.
I do not want to interrupt unduly, but the minister says this medical adviser can check the forms, can do this and can do that. Does he?

Yes; all the forms are most carefully checked in the light of the answers given by the first examining physician. Then, if there is still doubt, the man can be sent to a revision board. These boards consist of three doctors, and we are setting them up in different parts of Canada. Then, when the man is turned over to the training centre, he is examined again, this time by a military medical board in that centre. Once the man is delivered to the training centre he ceases to come under the jurisdiction of my department and comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence.
Would the minister give us some data, some figures, as to how many have been reexamined by other doctors, for instance, or by the board in each military district?
I do not know that I could give the number of reexaminations.
That is exactly what was asked.
The prime concern thus far has been to find men in the required categories, and there has been no difficulty in doing that. Up to now there has not been any object in reexamining all the rejects.
How many have been reexamined in each military district?
Not a great many of the rejects have been reexamined.

Naturally those who had been accepted would not be reexamined, except when they came to the training centres. No one but the rejects would be reexamined. Those who are accepted and automatically called up are examined at the training centre, as I understand it. I want to know how many of the rejects have been reexamined.

Not many of the rejects have been reexamined. It is only when the examination by the original physician indicates that perhaps an error has been made in the category, or where there is any doubt as to the category, that the man can be asked to report to another doctor. A further check has been made along these lines. In some instances reports have come in that a number of men were being rejected in a certain area by a certain doctor. These reports have been checked, and I am happy to say that I do not recall any instance in which it was found that a doctor was deliberately rejecting men or giving false information in these returns.
Could the minister give us information with regard to the men rejected, giving the percentage in each category, A, B and C?
Yes, I have that.
Could the minister give that by provinces, instead of for the whole of Canada?

It is given here by
administrative divisions. I have quite a long table, showing the number of men examined by civilian physicians, with the number and percentage in each medical category, for the first nine military training periods, given by administrative divisions. With the consent of the committee I could place this table on Hansard.
Is it very long?
It is quite a lengthy tabulation.

Before
placing it on Hansard, would the minister tell the committee the gross number of men examined by the civilian doctors, the number placed in each class, and the number rejected in each class? I think the desire is to get the number rejected in each class, in the first instance, to see just how 'bad or how good is the health of these young men.

Yes, I can give that. The total number of men examined for the first nine military training periods was 209,298. Of these, 116,800, or 55-9 per cent, were found to be in category A; 21,651, or 10-4 per cent, to be in category B-l; 8,265, or 3-9 per cent, in category B-2; 9,341, or 4-5 per cent, in category C-l; 11,575, or 5-6 per cent, in category C-2; 5,909, or 2-8 per cent, in category D, and 35,587, or 17 per cent, in category E.
The War-War Services
How many of those are unsuitable for military service? I do not know the technicalities well enough to know how many would be called.
My understanding is that the only ones taken for military training are those in category A.
That is right.

But I am not absolutely sure of that, because I have a recollection that some Bs and Cs were in the early months called for training. My recollection is-and I think I- am correct-that at present we are taking only category A men for actual training. They constitute 55-9 per cent of those examined by the civilian doctors.
The table to which the minister has referred is made out in divisions A, B, C and so on?
Yes.
Could the minister give the key in relation to military districts?

They do not absolutely check, but I could give a key which would be helpful. The divisions are named by letters of the alphabet. Division A has its headquarters at London, Ontario, and division B has its headquarters at Toronto.
Would the minister give the information also according to military districts? Can he do that? If he has not that information, I have it upstairs in my office, and could let him have it.
I could give the information respecting headquarters, and they check, roughly, although not exactly, with the military districts.
What number is A?

As the minister has stated, it is alarming to think that there should be such a large percentage of young men unfit for service. He went on to point out that plans were in contemplation for conditioning some of these young men who had been rejected. He should tell the committee just how far those plans have gone. For instance, are the men who have been rejected eligible for treatment in hospitals of the Department of Pensions and National Health?
No.
May they go in there and have operations which will enable them to qualify for the forces?
No, not yet.

What steps have been taken. It seems to me it is of vital importance to the nation that no steps should be spared which would enable those young men to qualify for the forces. It is not good enough to sit back, wring our hands and say that there is a heavy percentage who cannot qualify, and that we can do nothing about it. The health of many of those young men can be improved, and such improvement would be greatly to the benefit not only of the forces but also of the young men and their families, and of the nation at large. I would ask the minister to give a more detailed explanation of what the government has in mind in this connection.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South. The plans are just being formulated. I indicated that an interdepartmental committee was being set up, consisting of representatives of the Department of National Defence, the Department of Pensions and National Health, and the Department of National War Services.
With regard to the other question raised by the hon. member, these persons are not as yet entitled to any hospitalization or treatment. As he will appreciate, these men are still civilians who have not been turned over to the Department of National Defence. Therefore they are not yet soldiers. I assure my hon. friend that every effort will be made to study with the greatest possible care the plans necessary for the reconditioning of these men. I believe we shall be able to recondition quite a number, because a number of persons may be thrown into a category lower than that desirable for training, on account of some minor imperfection which could be remedied with comparatively little treatment. As is well known, the requirements for category A are quite severe.

When the minister is formulating his plans, wrould it be possible to include not only the men who come under the war service regulations but also the men who, although they do not come within the regulations, would be anxious to join the active service forces. I know a number of young men who have tried to join active service units, but who have been rejected as category E. For instance, some may require operations for hernia. In some instances the parents have been able to pay for operations, and the young men affected have gone overseas. In other instances young men in the same district remain in category E because they could not afford those operations. They may not come within the large group who would receive the reconditioning services outlined by the minister, but I believe they would have a claim to such reconditioning, even more than the men called under the regulations. When the minister is formulating his plans, could this point not be kept in mind?
Is my hon. friend thinking of persons who have applied for enlistment but have been rejected?
Yes.
We would be glad to give consideration to that suggestion.
I know there are a large number.

Mr. Chairman, I have a soft spot for the minister, because he has to take charge of all the matters his colleagues try to get rid of. That is a very hard problem for him, and I take this opportunity to pay him a well-deserved tribute by saying that he is equal to the occasion, and by pointing out that he is assisted in his work by two excellent deputy ministers, Mr. Justice Davis and Major-General LaFleche.
Very often young men try to enlist when they are unfit. They may be passed as class A by the local board and by the army medical board in the district. I see many people in my constituency, and I took the trouble to question some of these boys who had been placed in category A. To my great surprise I learned that men who had been placed in category A by two boards were suffering from such disabilities as ruptures, internal goitres and chronic appendicitis. This matter was referred to the board which found that these men should be in category E on account of disabilities which they possessed when they had their first examination.

The War-War Services
This shows two things. First, it shows that many French-Canadians are willing to enlist even though they are not physically fit and, second, it shows that the doctors are not always as careful as they should be. Apparently the local board relies upon the army board, while the army board thinks the local doctors, who know the family history from the medical point of view, are well informed. The result is that no one pays any real attention, each relying upon the other. There has been considerable improvement in this connection and now more care is paid to the examination. I do not see why the dominion government should waste money in training soldiers who are physically unfit. We all regret that such a large proportion of our soldiers are below standard as far as health is concerned and it is to be hoped that there will be an improvement in the near future.
I have only one question to ask the minister. There is one thing upon which I should like to congratulate him, something that I mentioned yesterday afternoon. I refer to the regulation passed by his department providing that those engaged in agriculture and the operations of railways shall be considered as being in seasonal occupations. Many of us know the necessary work that is being done by these workers, and I am glad to note that in an amendment dated October 4 of this year these occupations are listed as seasonal and essential. This should have been done in the original regulation, but the correction has been rightly and aptly made by the minister.
According to subsection 1 of article 14, as redrafted, it is provided that no postponement order may be made for more than six months, but upon reviewing the occupation the
board may grant one or more extensions, provided that the board may cancel the order at any time for military reasons or for cause. If it is established to the satisfaction of the commission that a man is serving the state by doing agricultural work or working as a railroad man, will a postponement be granted for a further six months, at which time he can report to the commission or to the registrar? Also, if the conditions are not changed at the end of six months, is a renewal of the postponement order authorized by the new regulations?

I think the regulations
are quite clear in that regard. My answer will be in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White). No postponement can be for longer than six months, but when that six months period is over, another postponement may be granted. The jurisdiction of the board is not confined to the second postponement; the board may grant one or more extensions of the original postponement, but each postponement must be for a period of not longer than six months. In each case the board looks at the application from the point of view of the national interest and deals with each case upon its merits. It has complete jurisdiction in granting or refusing an application for a postponement order.
Will the minister place upon the record the number of postponements granted in the different divisions?

I can do that, although
it is quite a lengthy table.

The minister said that each case discussed was considered by these boards' on its merits, and that the sole disposition of cases lay with the boards?
Yes.
Under this new regulation, national war service regulation No. 14, there is no longer any appeal to the minister, and, as I understand it, the sole disposition depends now upon the board in question.
Quite right.

Could the minister elaborate that to the committee, and explain what is done to arrive at some degree of standardization among the different boards. May I point out, for instance, a glaring example which was reported in the press some time ago. In Manitoba certain hockey players made application for postponement because they wanted to go to the United States to play hockey. Their applications were rejected, but in one of the other provinces-Ontario, I believe-some hockey players applied- for and received their permission.
It seems to me that the former regulation was preferable. This is a tremendous responsibility to leave in the hands of what is, after all, a quasi-judicial body not directly responsible to this house. It is possible that, if the personnel of a board were not of the right type, a state of petty tyranny might exist in a province. A person has no appeal to the minister or
to any other body. If the men on the board are unsympathetic or have not the proper approach to the problem, a very difficult local situation might arise. At the other extreme, in another administrative area there might be a very lax board and consequently an unsatisfactory situation. To confer sole jurisdiction and the unfettered disposition of these cases upon what should be only an administrative board is to set up a series of boards which have no standardized system of interpretation, can deal with each case in their own way, and may deal with these cases entirely differently in different geographical sections of the dominion. I wondered what system the minister had for standardizing the work of the boards right across the country, or is each board to be a law to itself, applying these regulations as it sees fit to each case that comes before it?

I think we should get one thing cleaned up at a time. We have asked for the numbers of applications and exemptions from each province. If the minister will put that information on the record, it will clear up that point.

The question which the hon. member for Weyburn has raised might also be raised with regard to our courts of justice when they are trying questions of fact, because the human element comes in there. I would remind the hon. member that each one of these administrative boards consists of three persons, and is headed by a judge of a superior court or other court of the province. In addition, there are two other representatives, and I think I can properly say that they are responsible men in their communities. Also, a representative of the Department of National Defence, and a representative of the national labour supply council, have the right to be present at the sittings of the board, and each of them has the right to make representations to the board. I believe I can safely say that the board deals with these applications for postponement carefully and judicially; I might go even further and say, sympathetically.
The hon. member for Weyburn asked about some hockey players, and the leader of the opposition also made some reference to them. I think this subject has received in the sports columns of the newspapers a great deal more attention than it deserves. I was in Toronto when the first announcement was made of the decision made by Mr. Justice Adamson, of administrative division J, who had had a number of young men appear before him to ask for his authority to leave Canada so that they might play professional hockey in the

United States. He rejected those applications. I was asked what my opinion of the matter was. and I expressed the opinion generally-I hold it yet-that the needs of the war supersede those of sport. I was also asked what would be the effect of that decision. As I have pointed out, in respect of these particular matters the chairman of each board has jurisdiction, and he may deal with the case in accordance with his views on the subject. The section which is involved in these applications by hockey players is section 4, subsection 2. I should like to put it on the record so that there may be the fullest understanding of this situation. It reads:
No male British subject who is liable to be called out for military training under the next preceding subsection shall, after bis age class has been called out by proclamation, as provided by subsection 1 of section 5 of these regulations, leave Canada for any reason whatsoever, unless and until he has been so authorized in writing by the chairman of the board to whose jurisdiction such man is subject.
Therefore anyone who is under twenty-one years of age does not have to go to the chairman of the board for necessary authorization in writing, nor does anyone who is over twenty-four, so that the chairman of the board deals only with applications coming from young men who are in the age groups that have been called up by proclamation, that is to say, young men of the 21, 22, 23 and 24 age classes.
The respective chairmen of the boards have dealt with this subject in a manner that is not altogether uniform, but I should point out that it is the chairman of the board who de'als with these applications for written authority to leave the country. It may be of interest to know, in view of the fact that so much publicity has been given to this matter in the sports pages of the newspapers, that altogether there are sixty hockey players who have been granted permission to leave Canada by the chairmen of the divisional boards: seven from adminstra-tive division A, London; twenty-two from administrative division B, Toronto; six from administrative division C, Kingston; four from administrative division D, Port Arthur; five from administrative division E, Montreal; one from administrative division F, Quebec; none from administrative division G, Halifax; one from administrative division H, Saint John; none from administrative division I, Charlottetown; none from administrative division J, Winnipeg; none from administrative division K, Vancouver; one from administrative division M, Regina; thirteen from administrative division N, Edmonton. I understand that the chairmen, in granting this written authority, to leave Canada in order to play hockey.

I do not know how one could get uniformity on questions of fact from administrative boards any more than one could get uniformity on questions of fact from courts of law. We are seeking as best we can to get uniformity in the matter of dealing with all those persons whose cases are considered by the board as individual persons, each person having his own case before the board. We have had conferences here at Ottawa by the chairmen of the boards, and that sort of thing has been helpful. I do not recall when we had the latest conference, but it was before I took charge of the department, and I think it might be useful to have another conference for the purpose of bringing about further uniformity of administration. I believe, however, I can say to the hon. member for Weyburn that where the human factor comes in, I do not see how one can eliminate differences altogether any more than one can in a court of law or in cases before juries. One jury might convict a man whereas another jury might acquit him, and they are trying questions of fact .and dealing with individual cases.	I can say this, however, that the
boards have sought to deal with these applications for postponement in a careful, judicial and sympathetic manner, and that, by and large, the regulations, from that point of view, have worked fairly satisfactorily.

I do not want to find fault with the regulations, but I do suggest two things. While it may not be possible to have complete uniformity, it is possible to have a greater measure of uniformity, because it is not altogether a fact-finding matter. As far as the public are concerned, here were men who had identical cases to 14873-270J
present. The minister himself has said that in Winnipeg men are rejected, whereas in London or Toronto men are given permission to proceed across the line. The difference was not in fact; it was in the interpretation given by the chairmen of the boards. It seems to me that if we want to have the public regard this as fair administration, we shall have to have a greater degree of uniformity; otherwise a man will feel that someone else living in another province with a different personnel on the board will get different treatment from what he gets in his particular district. The second suggestion I make is this. I still think the first regulation which allowed some court of appeal-either the minister or some official here-would obviate much of the feeling of uneasiness which has arisen in consequence of these different decisions that are handed down by the respective boards in identical cases.
If I understood the hon. member for Temiseouata correctly, he said that agriculture was included with lumbering as a seasonal occupation. Is that the view of the department?

Farming is dealt with under section 14 of the regulations, the heading of which is "seasonal and essential occupations." Therefore I think the interpretation placed on the matter by the hon. member for Temiseouata is reasonably sound, because farming is also named in the operative part along with a number of other occupations also of a seasonal and essential nature. I put the whole section on the record when I was before the committee previously.

In that connection I would point out that there may be sections of Canada in which agriculture could be properly classified as a seasonal occupation. Nevertheless there are wide areas where the word "essential" would be the proper description, because in large areas in Ontario, due to the care and feeding of live stock, the winter season is practically as busy on the average farm as the summer season.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the members of these boards which have had thrown upon them the responsibility of making the selection of those to take this military training. I think in some respects the considerations that have entered greatly into these decisions would be where dairy farms and farms where there is a heavy hog production may properly be classified as essential to our war effort. But I would point out that the beef cattle areas represent an equally important item of production as far as our war

The War-War Services
effort' is concerned, because wherever we have had a curtailment of consumption of pork products, beef is used to a greater extent as a substitute than any other commodity. Special attention should be given to that point.
Beef is important from another point of view. It is a staple commodity that enters into the diet of our army and our civilian population. Then, if we happen to have any surplus, there is ample provision for export to the United States, thus providing the much needed United States dollars to purchase vital commodities for the building up of our mechanized forces. Therefore the production of beef should be on a par with districts producing pork products and dairy products.
By this section the occupation of farming is put in exactly the same position as any occupation that is essential to the prosecution of the war.

I should not like to have this committee think that in provinces other than Ontario live stock can be grown without having help to feed it. Ontario is not the only province in Canada. While in Alberta we have very bright sunshine, we still have to do a great deal of work to raise that vastly increased crop of hogs that we have there at the present time. While in Alberta we raise four-legged hogs, I am sorry to say that in some of the provinces they raise the twolegged type.

A little while ago we were discussing the matter of men being rejected on account of being physically unfit. I notice on page 4100 of Hansard the minister is reported as saying:
Out of a total of 217,588 men examined up to October 2, 1941, only about 56 per cent were placed in category A, the only category accepted for training at the present time by the Department of National Defence. This is a serious situation, and the plans for the reconditioning of these men who have been '*rjected are under consideration.
For over 50 per cent of our young men in the prime of life to be physically unfit is indeed an alarming state of affairs. I do not think the minister would tell us this 50 per cent were physically unfit by reason of having ruptures, or appendicitis, or something of that kind. The old adage that "an ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure" still holds good. I am wondering whether something cannot be done to prevent the teen age boys who are coming along and who, if the war lasts two or three years more, will perhaps be called into service, from being also found physically unfit.

The minister said that plans for reconditioning these young men are under consideration.
I would implore the minister not to use the term "reconditioning".
It sounds like an old car.
Yes; men are not made of tin.

Will the hon. member
suggest a better term?

We talk of reconditioning machinery after it has been used. The term might be in order if we could say that these young men are physically unfit because they have been giving such strenuous service to the building up of Canada. I think, however,
I am right when I suggest that the reason why 50 per cent of our young men cannot pass the physical tests when they are called up for training is that for ten long years we have gone through a state of poverty and destitution which was deliberately imposed upon the country. We may say that times are better now, that people are earning more money, but can we say that is going to continue? I should like to ask the minister if he agrees with my diagnosis, that it is on account of the depression of recent years that these young men are not physically fit. I think the subject of malnutrition in these past years is worthy of attention.
I do not want to be jumping up and down, so, while I am on my feet, might I refer to another matter? The minister can keep in mind the question I have asked him so that he can answer later. The subject of broadcasting was brought up some little time ago, , and some discussion took place. On August 20 of this year I was very much alarmed to discover, in a newspaper which I picked up, that in a radio broadcast over the national network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a private member of this house had read a secret document that was in the hands of the intelligence service of this country. I say I was seriously shocked to read that in the newspaper, because I happened to be a member of the committee on the defence of Canada regulations before which that document was read. It was not shown to the members of the committee, which met in camera; it was read by an officer of the Department of Justice, and we did not even see it. Due to the fact that those sittings were held in camera I felt, as I believe other members of the committee felt, in duty bound to keep secret such matters as I have just mentioned. The committee concluded its work;' we went to our respective homes, and

then along comes a private member of parliament-who was also a member of that committee-who has been given access to these secret documents of state, who can take them out of the files and read them in a radio speech over a national hook-up.
I am not seriously complaining because the document was read. What I am complaining about is the fact that this was a secret document, read to a committee sitting in camera, and the members of that committee felt in duty bound to keep everything of that kind confidential. Then a private member is given access to it. I should like the minister to tell me by what authority this private member was given permission to obtain this document and read it over the radio.
