The first question asked by my hon. friend had reference to the very large number of persons who were rejected when they presented themselves for medical examination after being called up. While I appreciate that the situation is a very serious one, I should not like to go so far as to say that it is the result of the depression years. Those may have had their effect on some of these men, but I should like to point out that the standards set by the Department of National Defence are very high.
I should point out also that some of the ailments on account of which men were placed in categories lower than A were slight in themselves, but sufficient to exclude these men from the highest category, without in any way affecting their ordinary health. I wonder how many members of this house could get into category A.
We are not twenty-one year olds.

Even so, men may not be in category A and yet be in excellent health to all intents and purposes, without being able to undergo the very severe strains that must be undergone by soldiers. When I point out these things, of course I am not minimizing the grave nature of the problem.
What fee is paid to civilian doctors for these preliminary examinations? I undertsand that at the outset the fee was $1.
Yes.

If that fee is still paid, it seems to me that a very thorough examination cannot be expected for it. Have the doctors across Canada agreed to do this work for this small fee as part of their contribution to the war effort?
Yes.

Are they really conducting a $5 examination and thus making a contribution of $4 to the cause, or is only a superficial examination made? Perhaps the minister would enlarge upon the nature of the examination.

I think we can safely say that in a great many cases the doctors are doing this work as a contribution to the national effort. The fee they receive is $1 per examination, which is a great deal less than one would have to pay ordinarily for an examination of this kind. I believe they give a fair physical examination.

May I direct the minister's attention to a somewhat wider aspect of this question of man-power. He will recall that in the course of the remarks I made in the house a week ago to-day I referred to the question of Canada's potential man-power capacity, and to the national registration of August, 1940. I believe I have served sufficient notice, and I
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
should now like to have a specific statement of Canada's potential man-power capacity as disclosed by the national registration, not only for the armed services but for other classes of service as well. If the minister is not in a position to make the statement tonight, perhaps he would be good enough to make it to-morrow.
Does he agree with the statement made by his predecessor, as reported by the press, that Canada can muster a million men for the armed forces, and still attain the necessary production in farm and factory? I do not know whether or not that is possible, but I hope it is. There may have been a little bit of optimism on the part of the minister's predecessor, but I have no doubt that he made the statement in good faith, believing in the truth of it, because one would not suggest anything else from the present Minister of Agriculture.
The statement is not word for word what I said. I read it, of course, and I have it in writing.

The words I have used may not be the exact words used by the minister, but they are taken from the lead of the Canadian Press, and if they are in error, the Minister will correct them. I believe, however, that I have given the substance of what he has said. That is what the public understood him to say. I am not disagreeing with him; I am asking him for information.
The Canadian Press dispatch dated at Ottawa, September 13, states:
Canada can muster 1,000,000 men for the armed forces and still attain the necessary production in farm and factory, agriculture minister J. G. Gardiner said last night in a reconsecration week speech on the national network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

If 1.000.000 men were called to arms, he said, there would still be 7,000,000 persons over sixteen years of age left and these properly organized and determined to stand behind the armed forces can operate all our farms, our factories and places of business in a manner which will give us the production required.
The last sentence is what I said.

I do not rise to attack that statement. It may have been a slight exaggeration, but I should think it was at all events within shooting distance of being correct. I should hope it would be. This country paid a good many hundreds of thousands of dollars for the national registration, and it would have cost a great deal more had it not been for the voluntary

I used the words "young fools" in the sense of gaminerie. I could not find an exact translation of this word as we would use it in ordinary conversation. The nearest is boisterous or turbulent. I want to make this explanation in order to keep the record clear.

The minister in charge explained that one of the objectives of the national registration which was taken last year was to make it possible for people who were unemployed in one part of Canada to move to other areas where employment might be available. There are a great many men in the prairie provinces who were machinists or

mechanics before they took up farming. These men now find that they are producing what is often described as a drug on the market; they are producing wheat, which is apparently not needed at the present time. Many of these men are anxious to make some other contribution in the way of producing necessary commodities. So far, I have not met one who has been encouraged to move from western Canada to eastern Canada to find employment in industry. On the contrary, I know of men who are well qualified and who have written many letters in the hope of finding employment, but they have received no encouragement.
I should like the minister to explain just what use has been made of the national registration which was taken last year. Are the files kept up to date? Has the government information as to the number of toolmakers who are living in the prairie provinces and whose services could be used in eastern Canada?
The minister was to give me some information.

Questions have been coming from all quarters. Before I deal with the questions put by the leader of the opposition, I should like to put on Hansard a table showing comparisons between the administrative divisions and the military districts, along with the table I referred to when that question arose. The table is as follows:

I should like to deal in a general way with what has taken place with regard to the national registration.
I brought to the attention of hon. members the other evening, when I first spoke to the committee, a certain publication entitled "Specialized Occupations, National Registration, 1940", issued by the Department of National War Services and the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. All or practically all of the information requested by the hon. member for Mackenzie is contained in this particular book. Last year there was given by my predecessor a fairly full description of the manner in which the national registration had proceeded across Canada. When the cards came

The War-War Services
in to the Department of National War Services they came in by tons. The work of tabulating, compiling and getting the necessary statistical information together was assigned to the bureau of statistics. The bureau has been working on that, and this spring, I believe, was responsible for the publication of this book which I have mentioned. Perhaps the best thing I can do is to read the preface, which is brief, and then indicate the kind of information which is found in this book. The preface, written by the dominion statistician, Doctor R. H. Coats, is, in part, as follows:
The national registration was conceived and carried out primarily as a register of the military and labour potential of Canada. In accordance with this conception, the main tasks assigned to the dominion bureau of statistics, in addition to .the revision and permanent filing of the registration cards as received from deputy registrars, have been:
1.	The selection of single males of military age.
2.	The listing of persons in some 1,250 specialized occupations.
3.	The listing of persons with training in agriculture.
4.	The selection of certain classes of aliens, and
5.	The compilation of a general conspectus of the ages, birthplace, nationality, education, etc., of the Canadian adult population.
The first of these involved the transfer of some 1,050,000 cards for the use of the Department of National Defence.
These are cards that came back to our department and are available to be sent out to the various administrative divisions, so that when we issue a proclamation calling out a particular age class or a series of age classes, all of the cards relating to those persons are sent to the administrative divisions and are there in the custody of the registrar.
The second and third and fourth were made by the construction of lists giving the addresses and various personal and occupational information for about 2.200,000 names. These have been placed at the disposal of .the departments and others requiring such information.
The first four objectives have now been achieved. In addition, preliminary tabulations concerning the fifth part, which was not undertaken until the listing process above-mentioned was completed, have now been published in bulletin form.
In this publication to which I have made reference there is an introduction which explains the set-up of the various tables and deals with this subject of 1,250 specialized occupations. The persons who are in those specialized occupations totalled about 1,800,000 across Canada. There are a number of tables in this publication which will give a good deal of the information asked by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Mackenzie.
I think I may also say that the subject of man-power generally is being carefully studied.
Another publication to which I made reference is entitled "Statistics Relating to Labour Supply under War Conditions." That was issued by the social analysis branch of the dominion bureau of statistics.
Since registration took place, there has been a continuing registration of all persons who have reached the age of sixteen, who are required to register as soon as they do reach that age. Then, all changes of address and of matrimonial status are recorded. The system of keeping track of these cards and of this information is such that, I think I can say to the committee that if I were asked to locate a certain man or woman who had registered, it could be done, by the system which they have there, in just a few minutes. The records are in excellent shape.
With regard to the question of the hon. member for Mackenzie as to the moving of men from one district to another, thus far that has not -taken place under government direction except in an indirect way. Nor does it take place in the old country, where they have a system which enables them to send men to one industry, or away from one industry to another. Although the power of compulsion is there, they have not exercised it. They have directed labour, and they have done that largely through the operations of the employment offices. As hon. members will recall, we did not have dominion government employment offices set up until recently, and we are of opinion that, if any movement of labour is required from one area to another to meet the needs of industry in any locality, the establishment of the new employment offices will be very helpful to us in directing that flow of labour from one place to another.

I followed the minister closely, and I am aware that there is a great deal of valuable material available, but I do not think members of parliament have received this' report which he mentioned. If that is so, then I wonder how many firms in industry are making any use of the information which has been compiled. I might remind the committee that so far we have had practically no expenditures for capital equipment in connection with the providing of -any war industries in western Canada-certainly, in the province of Saskatchewan. I know that a great many people have come to the east from Saskatchewan, but men who wait for encouragement or for advice as to the possibility of getting employment should they come east, simply never come. I realize that there are many difficulties, but it seems to me that so far nothing has been done except to discourage people from coming. The hon. member for

[DOT]4290
The War-War Services

Weyburn has handed me a clipping from a western paper dated October 23, a dispatch from Windsor by the Canadian Press which reads:
Stay west, young man, says mayor. Windsor chief magistrate warns prairie folk to keep away. No work available. Bad advice being given by social service agencies.
Canadian Press. Windsor, Ont., Oct. 23- Premiers of the three prairie provinces will be asked to -warn residents of their provinces that there is no employment available here, Mayor Arthur J. Reaume said Wednesday following receipt of reports from industries here that large numbers of men from western Canada were seeking jobs. Forty-five in one day.
Mayor Reaume said 45 Saskatchewan men appeared at one large plant seeking work Tuesday. Industries throughout the city have reported four and five men from the prairie provinces have appeared at their employment offices daily during the past week and had to be turned away, the mayor said.
"I am told that they said they were advised by social service agencies in Saskatchewan and the other prairie provinces that there were jobs to be had here," Mayor Reaume said. ''This is not the case and it is time the people of the prairie provinces were warned that they were wasting their money by coming to Windsor looking for work . . ."
Letters will be sent to the mayors in the leading cities of the three provinces as well as to the premiers, the mayor added.
I understand that letters covering the same information have been sent to the municipalities in western Canada. I suggest it is time now that some machinery be made available so that men who are trained or who are willing to be trained may have an opportunity to make some contribution apart from that which they are making in producing wheat or by being on relief. In large areas in the west there have been crop failures and there are many men who will have to depend upon the government for assistance. We should be making use of the labour power that is available. I had expected that the minister would have something more hopeful to say in connection with the employment of men who are well trained and who could make a contribution in industry.

I have one or two questions to' ask the minister. A short time ago when he was giving a summary of the various exemptions that had been granted, he classed them under farming, lumbering, fishing, and so on, and I understood him to say that under the head of "miscellaneous" there were some 7,000 or 8.000. May I ask under which class university students are included? In putting that record on Hansard, could he indicate the number of university students who have been granted exemptions? Would he also give the committee a brief statement indicating what constitutes a university

student? Does it mean a man who is attending university so many hours each day, or does it mean that he may be taking one or two lectures a week, or would it include any man who is taking a course by correspondence? Would such a man be classed as a university student and be given exemption? Would the minister care to express an opinion as to whether exemptions such as these are class legislation?

The number of postponements in connection with university and college students, requested for the first three periods, is 971; applications granted, 892. Then, for the remaining periods, four to nine, the postponements requested number 1,371 and those granted, 1,236. Section 17 of the regulations contains the following subsection, 10:
The board may grant a postponement order to a student who is registered at a Canadian university or college to follow a course leading to a degree or diploma and who has been accepted by the university or college authorities.
There are a number of other regulations regarding students, but I do not consider that as preferred treatment. I think it is desirable that bona fide students should be entitled to have postponement of military training during the terms of their college yeaTS. Many of them belong to other compulsory military training units in their universities or in the Canadian officers training corps, and I do not think any preferential treatment is given to these persons.

I understand that in the 21-year-old class, owing to lack of accommodation, between 40 and 60 per cent of the young men available have been called. If that is correct, will the minister state clearly to the committee how the registrars make the selection and who would be picked in the 40 or 60 per cent of the young men called.

That was the question which the leader of the opposition put to me and which I have not yet had an opportunity of answering. I should be glad to try to answer it. The Department of National War Services receives a requisition each month from the Department of National Defence indicating the number of persons whom the Department of National Defence requires for the next training period. That is broken up by the Department of National Defence into the number who are required from each administrative division. The registrar of the administrative division gets these instructions, and his duties are to distribute the number of notices to the various parts of his division, as fairly and equitably as he can. He proceeds in this way. He starts first of all with the lowest

The War-War Services
age group. He takes the 21-year class and, going still further, he takes first of all the persons who were born earliest in that particular year.
It goes by seniority.

Or juniority, if I may say so. In addition to that, an attempt is made to work out an equitable distribution between persons who have never been called up for any period of training and persons who either did their thirty-day training and are called again or persons who had become twenty-one previously and whose applications for postponement were granted. In that way an effort is made to place the men who are subject to call as equitably as possible over the whole administrative division over which the registrar has jurisdiction. It is done on the basis of age groups and working out an equitable division between the new twenty-ones and the old twenty-ones. The system is not perfect, but an effort is made to work it out.
Under that system no one should escape being called?
No.
Everybody in the 21-year-old class so far has been called?

I do not think so. I do not think we have exhausted all the twenty-ones even yet. But I do not think there is any likelihood of any escaping being called, because the cards are all there in the administrative divisions.

This point of the call brings me to something on which I desire to make an observation and to ask the minister whether he thinks anything can be done about it; that is the practice of calling the twenty-one year olds, the twenty-twos, and I understand the proclamation now includes those up to twenty-four, but only the twenty-ones and the twenty-twos have been called up.
They are all subject to the proclamation.

I would suggest to the government through the minister that while the idea of calling them by age groups one year at a time beginning with the twenty-one year group was perhaps valid when we conceived the idea of thirty-day training, so that the matter would go on progressively and everyone between the ages of twenty-one and forty-five who was eligible would ultimately get training, yet that practice lost its validity, I think, when we switched to what is virtually training for the duration.
I have some recollections of what happened to the generation of boys of that age in the last war, and I am fearful that if we proceed in this way we are again going to denude the country of the young men of a generation. It is simple to say that taking them for a period of training for the defence of Canada -and for the moment Canada is not in immediate danger of attack-causes less disruption to the general life and industry of the country. But I do not think that is sound either from the point of view of the army or, what -is perhaps more important at the moment, from the point of view of the country now or in the time to come.
I would suggest that the minister consider the idea of turning the list upside down; at any rate, if they will not go to the top, that they push up men from, say twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine to thirty-five or thirty-seven, even up to forty if not forty-five, and begin to take in not only single men but married men, taking at the beginning perhaps only married men with no families or with small families. When I think of the days when this thing will be over, I am sure that we are making a mistake in not dividing the responsibility over a wider group. I am perhaps selfish also in my thought that we should go into these higher brackets. If there is any group of men in Canada to-day who are "dodging the column"-it is not my duty to say at this time and place that there are- it is the men who were just too young for the last war and who to-day are comfortably employed, perhaps have homes partly paid for. small families, men who. as a rule, are in a fairly good income group and, in most instances, doing useful service. With a good conscience and the best will in the world thousands of them have hesitated to volunteer and put off on the shoulders of their wives and families the financial responsibilities that they have assumed. They are perhaps waiting until the day comes when they will be urgently required and these things will not matter. I think we might help some of these men to make a decision by expanding instead of restricting the groups called up under this proclamation. I think we should distribute the call more fairly across the face of the country and across the age groups.
As far as I am personally concerned I regard as of primary value in this training programme the fact that it does bring to the active service of the country a class of men who are highly desirable, in most instances, for active military service wherever they may be sent. I am of opinion that the sense of responsibility engendered in those older people would be of great value. I do not wish to suggest that any lack
The War-War Services

of responsibility is felt by the younger groups, because I say quite frankly that very many of the men who passed through my hands in the last two and a half months have been nearer eighteen than twenty-one. We do not ask for a birth certificate. I am not in the recruiting business anyway, but I see them shortly after they are in. We can now take a man in at eighteen; he likes to be a man at eighteen, and most of them are manly men, but in my opinion the distribution is not fair, neither is it wise, nor does it get the result for which, as far as I am concerned, we are looking.
No doubt the minister will say that the number called is the responsibility of the Minister of National Defence, and his job is to get them when they are wanted. I hope, however, the minister will not be satisfied merely to do his full duty, but will bring to bear whatever weight he can on the Department of National Defence to emphasize the necessity of getting, not a lesser number into training, but more.
If you come to the ultimate position and the Department of National Defence answer that they do not know what to do with those who do not become absorbed into the active service forces after they are trained, perhaps we are not too proud to take a leaf out of Hitler's book. We are told that he has a force of over half a million who, when he gets into a tight spot, he calls from industrial pursuits and puts into uniform. I am told that there are groups who have been so called out two or three times, and later returned to duty in industry; if it is only a story, there is the germ of an idea in it.
The training of men for this war cannot be left until three months before they are needed. I do not believe it is possible to train a soldier for the technical warfare of to-day in less than nine months and give him a Chinaman's chance for life. If we continue to carry on for a time without casualties as we have done so far, if the war does not break into an active campaign, perhaps by adding to the numbers in training we might train men in relays and reabsorb some into industry. In any event, however, it seems to me that we are not taking the full opportunity to use this service.
I am tempted-but I shall not yield to the temptation-to enlarge further on the question of general training in connection with the active service army, but I again urge on the minister that with which I started, namely, that the country be not denuded of the 20-, 21-and 22-year-olds, without taking a fair mixture of those in the higher ages, and I suggest that the government seriously consider the policy of taking some married men.

I listened
to the hon. member expounding his theoiy of calling up men. I do not know whether he has had to do with the training or simply the calling up of the men. But as one who has had something to do with the training of men, I must say that the idea of calling up men of the ages of thirty-seven to forty-five, with the strenuous training they have to go through, is absolutely out of the question. I have had a number of men, even in their early thirties, who could not stand the training that is required. We all know that this is a young man's war. I think we all agree that it is not a good thing for the country to have our young men spending the best years of their life in the army, but in a situation like this it has to be done; no one else can take their places. Men who are forty-five or forty-two or thirty-seven years of age cannot take the places of young men of nineteen, twenty or twenty-one in a war of this kind. It is not an old man's war; it is not a war of middle-aged men. Of course, as a last resort, I suppose men in the older brackets could be called up later on; I presume that is why the age limits were fixed at twenty-one to forty-five. These men might be called up for home defence, or something like that; but while my hon. friend's idea is very good in theory, I am sure it would never work out in practice.

I do not think I am discussing an abstract theory, but I am not going to engage in a contest. I did not suggest, however, that we should turn the list upside down and take all the men from the top instead of from the bottom. I do know that there are thousands of jobs, even in this army, which can be filled by old men of thirty-seven years of age. I would not put them in the mechanized forces, and I could not get them into the branch headed by the air minister, but there is a place for them. My thought is that we are not beginning to utilize their services but are robbing the other age groups. I have some knowledge of what people in their thirties can stand; I know better than to urge that they should be placed in competition with young men of nineteen, twenty and twenty-one years of age, but even in a young army I believe there should be a little adjustment of the scale. Let us not shift the burden quite so heavily to the shoulders of the boys; let us not only give the others a chance but see to it that they take that chance.

I am glad to hear this
exchange of views between the hon. member for Winnipeg South and the hon. member

The War-War Services
for Royal. I believe the general view was that it would be preferable to call out the younger men because this would cause the least dislocation in the economy of the nation; but following this interesting exchange of conflicting opinions I should like to give the matter careful consideration. Would the hon. member for Royal mention the ages up to which he believes the proclamation might be extended, if that should be thought wise? Do I understand his view to be that young men and older men might be mixed in the calling up?

As the minister knows, there is a certain syllabus of training that has been laid down, covering physical training, rifle exercises and drill for long periods. Naturally the younger men would stand up to it, but if a class of men from thirty-five to forty years of age should be called out at some later date, the syllabus of training could be changed in order that these men might be used for home service.
Men of thirty-five years of age are at present exempted from physical training.
Would the syllabus have to be changed to make it suitable for the older men?

Yes; the syllabus would have to be changed. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South when he says that older men could take the places of many younger men, particularly in office work. I believe here in Ottawa there are hundreds of young men of military age who should be released for overseas service, while older men of thirty-five to forty-five years of age could be used here and in every district throughout Canada. They could serve as cooks, clerks and so forth. I understand that the women's auxiliary army is to be used for these purposes, but the older men could be used as well. Then the young men could be relieved for service overseas or active service in Canada-frankly I do not think very much of this active service in Canada, though I am not going to elaborate on that now-and the more strenuous work of fighting. I believe some scheme could be worked out by the defence department and the war services department whereby we could utilize the services of the younger men for the more strenuous work, while the older men could perform the less arduous duties. I believe training could be adjusted to suit the age of the men called up; this should be a simple matter.

As one of those in the so-called awkward age, who was too young for the last war and apparently is too old for this one, it hurts a bit when, in a conscientious endeavour to do what one can for his country in a military way, he is told flatly either that he is too old or that he lacks military experience. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South that a place should be found for men in what I can only call the awkward age, whether it be doing office work or whether it be in the specialized branches of the army such as the ordnance or the paymaster's corps. I know a great many men object to going into those branches. One hon. member suggests "the kitchen," but I think our army is pretty well equipped in that respect. The fact remains that there are many, many men between the ages of thirty-five and forty-two, we will say, who want to do more than they are permitted to do under the present regulations, and I think the minister would be well advised to take into consideration some of the suggestions that have been advanced to-night. I for one heartily approve them, and I believe the result of getting such men in the army would be most encouraging.

What is the position with regard to young men who are not British subjects? There must be many thousands of young men domiciled here, earning their living in this country and probably intending to remain here all their lives, who are not citizens. Are they not subject to any kind of call?

Of course they were all subject to registration, but they have not been made subject to call for military training, even for home defence. The regulations apply only to:
. . . every male British subject who is or has been at any time subsequent to the first day of September, 1939, ordinarily resident in Canada while he is of the ages of twenty-one years to forty-five years inclusive, and who was, on the fifteenth of July, 1940, unmarried or a widower without child or children.
Therefore aliens are not subject to these regulations. I have checked this particular matter with the similiar provision in the United States draft law, and while in the United States everybody whether an American citizen or an alien, must register-and that provision is the same as we have in Canada,- in the United States they make subject to their draft law only American citizens and aliens who have indicated their intention of applying for American citizenship. I believe that is the language of the statute in the United States. Therefore even there they have

The War-War Services
gone perhaps a little further than we have in calling upon persons who have indicated their intention of becoming United States citizens. But they do not call aliens, other than the ones I have mentioned, any more than we do.

I suggest to the minister
that this is one policy which should be changed, particularly because here in Canada we are trying to recruit our army for overseas on a voluntary basis. We are asking young men to enlist, and quite often we are met with the answer, "Why should I enlist, and a young chap who is not a British subject be in a position to take my job?" Here are these young men who are not British subjects, but who earn their living in this country, and they are not even called up for the defence of Canada.
Surely they could be called up for that. If not that, then at least they could be called to do road work, or something of that kind to help the nation. How can we ever expect to raise a large volunteer army if these other men have to assume no burden whatsoever for the defence of the country in a time of crisis like the present? Can the minister say how many thousands of these young men there are?

I think that information is available somewhere. I cannot find at the moment the information as to the number of aliens, but I can assure the hon. member for Vancouver South that the question of whether aliens should be made subject to these regulations has received careful attention. It is quite clear that the argument advanced by the hon. member this evening, that British
subjects ordinarily resident in Canada are called for military training while aliens are left free to make big wages in the factories, has been made.
I am inclined to think that if we applied the regulation to aliens, we could apply them only to friendly and not to enemy aliens. No one would think for a moment of making enemy aliens subject to the regulations. Then, if we made the regulations applicable only to aliens who are not enemy aliens, we would not have a satisfactory condition. If only enemy aliens are given the opportunity to stay at home and earn big wages, while the others are subject to military training, there would be dissatisfaction. We have not thus far made the regulations applicable, except to British subjects ordinarily resident in Canada, and I am inclined to think that on balance the argument is in favour of the course we have adopted.
I have here the statement showing by nationalities and by provinces the number of non-British subjects between the ages of 21 and 45, both inclusive, who registered in Canada in August.
Single, or widowers without children?
Yes. Between the ages of 21 and 45.
It includes married men.

According to the heading I have here. From European countries, the total is 19,481; from American countries, 7,122, and from Asiatic countries, 1,126. The table is as follows:

Department of National War services.

Why could enemy aliens not be used on road work? In Saskatchewan at the present time Doukhobors, Mennonites and other conscientious objectors are use in the Prince Albert national park to build roads. Why could enemy aliens not be used for that purpose, if not in the army itself?

I suppose it would be possible to use them, if we put them, under a guard. But whether that would advance the war effort is quite another matter. They could be put to work, but whether it would be economical to do so is another matter.

I do not think the minister appreciates the seriousness of the question.

The War-War Services
Any enemy aliens who are dangerous to Canada should be interned, if they are not already interned. The others are not dangerous to Canada, and surely could be used to do road- work. Aliens who are not enemy aliens could surely be used for home defence or, if necessary, they, too, could be used for road work. But I do not see how the government can sit back and be complacent about this subject. Out in the ridings we are meeting it every week. The complaint is made time and again: "Why should my boy enlist when an alien does not need to do anything? Why should my boy have to lose his job, only to come back here to find an alien in his place receiving an increased salary, and leaving no chance for my son to get work?" Those things are happening in the country.
No doubt about it.

The ministry should not sit back, wash their hands of the question and say, "Oh, everything is1 all right, on balance; we think it is as well to carry on the way we are doing." It is for reasons like that the government is having trouble in getting recruits, and it will never get them in greater numbers until it tackles questions such as this with a great deal more determination. Here is one way in which recruiting across Canada could be helped. I do urge that the minister ought not to be satisfied to argue himself or to permit himself to be argued by the other ministers into the position of saying, "Oh, well, this question is taken care of well enough; just leave it alone, and carry on the way we are doing." The ministers are living in a fool's paradise if they think they can raise recruits while things like this are going on in Canada.
What was done in the conscription act of 1917? Were non-British subjects called to the colours, or called to do any other service for Canada at that time?
I do not think so.

I do not. think we can liken this war to the war of 1914-18, because this is not a war where national boundaries have played the same part as they did at that time. There are persons here from enemy countries who are as much anti-nazi and anti-fascist as Canadians could possibly be. Until the nations fighting fascism and nazism learn to utilize the services and the will to destroy nazism of all those people who are opposed to it, we are not going to succeed very fast. We are doing that, of course, in the countries overrun by nazis, and possibly in the nazi and fascist countries themselves.
I think there are various means that could be taken to protect foreign persons who are not naturalized Canadians and bring them to the point where they would be at least potential Canadian or British subjects. After they had been in the country for some time they should be compelled to indicate their intention of becoming Canadian citizens, and after they had indicated their intentions their services could be used.
I should like to draw the attention of the committee to a situation on the west coast. There we have many Canadians of oriental or Asiatic origin, many of whom have indicated their desire to enlist in the armed forces of the country, to serve wherever they could be used, and their offers have been refused. Why should the services of these people not be used? They wish to give their services, if necessary their lives, in defence of the country which is theirs either by birth or by naturalization.

I suppose that would be
because they would not come within the definition I mentioned a moment ago, namely, British subjects ordinarily resident in Canada.
They are British subjects; they were either born in Canada or have been naturalized.
Does the hon. member want to give the Japs the vote?

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) would like to make a statement, and I wonder if we could have a recess in this question period.
The committee rose and obtained leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house.

subtopic: POSTPONEMENT OF EFFECTIVE DATE FROM NOVEMBER 17 TO DECEMBER 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that on the recommendation of the war-time prices and trade board the government has decided to postpone the effective date of the maximum prices regulations from November 17 to December 1. The reason for the postponement is to ensure the most effective possible administration and enforcement of the regulations from the moment they come into operation. No change in policy is involved. The board is anxious to have a complete organization equipped and ready to deal with any kind of problem or difficulty which may arise when the new price policy goes into effect. Considerable progress
Questions

has already been made, but there remain some important appointments of necessary commodity administrators to be made, and the organization of staff is not yet complete.
Mr. Hector McKinnon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, informs me that careful consideration is being given to the many questions which have been raised by all sections of the public. The board regards it of the highest importance that the new policy should come into operation in a manner which will enable the public, both buyers and sellers, to be given promptly all necessary information, answers to questions, and decisions with regard to the many problems which are bound to arise. The board has accordingly made the recommendation to the minister to defer the date of commencement to December 1.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
Wednesday, November 12, 1941
